“It’s called the Republic of Sakha, or Yakutia—the name of the territory is actually under dispute. Under Russian authority, it’s been referred to over the years variously as the Republic of Sakha, or the Autonomous Republic of Sakha. However, the independence fighters refer to the area as Yakutia. There have long been rumblings for independence from the indigenous Sakha/Yakut people, but it wasn’t until the ethnic Russians, who’ve dominate the region for centuries, decided they want independence from Moscow that the conflict really boiled over. These Sakha Russians took on the mantle of Yakut independence in their propaganda, but generally treat the indigenous Yakuts as a political soccer ball. “

“Thus the sides, broadly speaking, are: Moscow-loyalist Russians vs Pro-independence Sakha Russians. Today, you might think ironically, most Yakuts are against independence. Yakut ethnic extremism was once a rare, very fringe phenomenon, but when it did happen, it tended to be very violent. However, in the decade before the Sakha rebellion, the Yakuts were radicalized by neighboring Buryats whose own independence movement flared on and off for years before burning out with no resolution due to sheer exhaustion of forces.”

“Despite promises to the contrary, Yakuts generally fear that the Sakha Russians will gain even more power in an independent state. The Russians are the descendants of settlers, some of whom harbored lingering resentment over Moscow’s limitation of their local control.” 

“On the other hand, some indigenous Yakuts, especially young men, do side with the independence movement and form a large chunk of the fighters. Although it’s hard not to suspect that at this point, many of them must realize they’ve gotten in over their heads.”

“Various other Siberian ethnic minorities have mostly tried to stay neutral, although individuals might side with one group or another.” 

“The (thoroughly russified) Itelmen, for example, tend to side with Moscow. The Evens mostly side with the Yakut indigenes.”

“The Koryaks/Chukchis to the east seem to have largely tried to keep out of the fray since the ceasefire in Magadan created a delicate situation there. The republics to the east, although they have nominally made their peace with Moscow, are separated from the motherland by a vast war zone. They’re supposed to be administered by Russian authorities, but there’s so much so-called ‘assistance’ from China that they’re arguably occupied by now. But that’s a whole different story.”
 
“Beyond the main conflict, a variety of other players have been involved, and the independence movement is only the nexus of a continent-wide political and social upheaval. You could equate it to the Arab Spring, or the Revolutions of 1848. I don’t know if anybody has given it a name. Probably somewhere in the scholarship they have. I’d call it ‘The Siberian Awakening’.”

“So, all of this has left the infrastructure in Sakha and surrounding areas in ruins, providing an opening for rival powers in the broader region. Especially China. Like I said, the far eastern regions of Siberia remain nominally loyal to Moscow, the conflict zones have effectively cut them off from western Russia.”

“But there’s a power vacuum now, and Chinese interests know how to exploit a power vacuum. The People’s Republic has maintained official neutrality, but the government hasn’t been entirely covert about encouraging Chinese nationals to take advantage of trade opportunities in the now cut-off areas. They call these policies ‘emergency trade rules’ and assert they are only in place for humanitarian reasons. And there’s a good argument that they’re providing a much-needed lifeline to the region.” 

“In practice, however, the policies seem to be an effort to undermine Russian authority and assure Chinese domination in the post-conflict world, no matter which side ends up winning. The reality on the ground is that the vast majority of so-called ‘Chinese trade envoys’—which are ostensibly supposed to be private merchants encouraged to open up trade routes into Russian territories—but are, in fact, members of organized crime groups whose most obvious activity—‘hostess clubs’ aka brothels—are to some extent just fronts for moving resources and stolen goods out of Russian territory.”

“Diamonds are the most obvious example, but everything from various mineral ores to jewelry and silverware are essentially being extracted. It’s a veritable torrent of goods over the border. You can see ‘Sell Your Gold’ signs all over the cities, from Vladivostok to Anadyr.”

“And as the valuables flood out, flooding in are arms, drugs, armies of sex workers, enormous gambling establishments, and liquor.”

“Most notoriously knock-off airag. They call it tar or kymys or ayran, but what it is is fermented mare’s milk. Or at least, mare’s milk is the traditionally favored variety. It’s often mass-produced with cow’s milk though. And laced with formaldehyde, heavy metals, and who knows what else. A lot of the milk comes from cattle raised in Ningxia, in the exclusion zone around the Ganshu Baiyin reactor. These ‘emergency trade rules’ have allowed Chinese exporters to skirt traditional trade restrictions.” 

“Along with the crime, an increasingly large transfer of population from China is happening as roadside stands become permanent fixtures. There are now Chinatowns in towns and cities all through Primorskiy Krai and Amur, up into Khabarovsk. More troubling are up-and-coming Triad leaders who basically take over small villages with their newfound economic muscle. In the countryside located well away from the hottest conflict zones. When I was there, it wasn’t an uncommon occurrence to see parades of SUVs celebrating a young Chinese mobster’s wedding to an even younger Siberian bride, rolling past brand new McMansions with freshly-filled in ground pools.”

“In contrast to the Chinese interest in solidifying central Asian hegemony, the Japanese government has maintained a truly hands-off approach. But not to be outdone, Japanese organized crime has taken a keen interest in the area. Centering on Vladivostok, the Triads have set up a similar array of grey- and black-market activities. Since their interest in eastern Siberia is really just a cover for involvement further west in Sakha, the Triads don’t really care, so long as they keep their activity restricted to the southeastern coastal area. They’ve had historical activities in these areas, and the Triad seem to be giving them free reign for now. A visitor could be forgiven for believing that the Yakuza now ruled Vladivostok outright. So within that narrow strip along the coast extending from Amurskiy Bay south of Vladivostok, up and around to Tugur, it’s truly starting to resemble the Wild West. Unfortunately, or fortunately depending upon your point of view, the area is rapidly developing. There are mineral boomtowns and fishing ports drawing migrant workers from far inland. All run by the Yakuza, though they rarely venture farther inland than the Republic of Amur.”

“Japan has practically repossessed Sakhalin Island.”

“But as the conflict drags on, an additional wrinkle has emerged. Chinese Triads have ceased to be satisfied with restricting their own activities to the conflict zone proper, and have expanded southwards into Mongolia, along the main contraband thoroughfares, and east towards the coast. Recently, it’s becoming increasingly clear clear that there is a simmering turf war between the Chinese and Japanese gangsters. The Chinese have thus far kept the Triads on a short leash for the sake of international diplomacy, but their newfound legitimacy has some of the bosses talking of ‘cleaning up’ the east coast. They say that somebody needs to crack down on crime, and they’ve got contacts in the police forces across the region. If that happens, we’re talking small town Russian police units that are transparently puppets of the highest of Chinese gang leaders sweeping into the new boom towns along the coast to tackle Yakuza leaders on their own turf. It’ll be a nightmare.”

“Until this development, it seemed the interests of organized crime generally aligned with each other, apart from mild competition. Chinese Triads want some order because they rely upon an effective infrastructure to move massive amounts of contraband, but they thrive under diminished rule of law. Similarly, Japanese Yakuza like the relative order of eastern Kamchatka, outside the war zones to the west. But they need the Triads to remain occupied in the conflict zones so they don’t get pushed out by gangsters drawing support from larger Chinese power centers. The long term goal of the Triads—and perhaps the Yakuza—is to have the the Sakha government firmly in their pockets, regardless of whether Moscow wins, or the Rebels win” 

“Where’s the international rule of law in all this?” Asked Mrs. Stang. “In my day, the UN would have stepped in.” 

“Well, NGOs have had a limited humanitarian impact because the Chinese government has argued their own efforts at encouraging trade are sufficient. To their credit, the Party really has actually underwritten many of the itinerant merchants who’ve been able to supply most staples and durable goods. If it weren’t for that, we might be seeing a humanitarian crisis of epic proportions.” 

“Whether this underwriting really and truly translates into lower prices, as is claimed. Well, that’s a matter of widespread debate. Of course, the PRC’s ulterior motives are fairly apparent. Like I said, they want their foothold in Sakha to become economic dependence. And they’ve generally argued their case successfully, above the concerns raised by many NGOs. At least, to the satisfaction of most world leaders, anyway.”

“So, instead of providing humanitarian aid, NGOs have mostly focused on conflict resolution and communication support. Like me.” 

“When I was there, the major player in the Republic of Sakha itself, was the ARSDC, the Almazy-Rossii Sakha Diamond Company. They vowed strict neutrality, but widespread opinion is that they’re playing all sides. Along with humanitarian NGOs, Almazy-Rossii is among the few entities who have official dealings with both the Moscow authorities and the Sakha provisional government. ARSDC is trying to consolidate its monopoly, but management conflicts have left the company teetering on the edge of a breakup. They’ve been determined to continue production, and they hire partisans from both sides. After all, since the outbreak of open conflict, their near-poverty wages have been considered a very good deal for the impoverished workforce. Their operations are scattered across eastern and central Siberia, and they are the closest thing to a neutral zone in the region. The Mirna Diamond Mine is the company’s primary regional home base. We used to schedule meetings between the rival powers in their conference room there.”

“Us expats in the NGO crowd used to pronounce ARSDC as ‘Arse-Dick’. They were useful, but didn’t have a very good reputation.”

“There’s also been a huge demographic shift as populations have fled the area, while other populations have streamed in. Sakha has become increasingly Yakut indigenes as Moscow-loyal ethnic Russians have fled westward. Ironically, the remaining Sakha Russians have tightened their grip on power in the Republic as the de facto government has claimed greater and greater wartime powers.” 

“Interestingly, there has been a dramatic increase in Koryak population. That started before the conflict, because warming-driven expanded grazing lands led to a resurgence in traditional pastoralism.”

“Sorry, at this point, I’m just regurgitating my orientation class textbooks.”

“Go on,” she said. 

“Well, more and more Koryaks—who had become a thoroughly urban population in the previous generations—they sought to return to the traditional lifestyle. It was kind of a dream for a lot of them. They’d often mortgage their houses and pawn valuables to purchase reindeer and yaranga materials—yurts. This return to the land movement coincided with, many young couples chosing to have more children, to complete the traditional lifestyle. For the first time in living memory, the Koryak population experienced a baby boom.”

“But the traditional ways require traditional wisdom. Very of those new families were able to transition successfully into self-sufficiency. They looked for ways to keep solvent. Some re-selling their reindeer as meat. Some tried dairy. Reindeer kymys, faux-traditional crafts for tourists in urban centers, whatever they could do to turn a ruble. But a sudden glut in the market, combined with a decrease in tourism due to the conflict in neighboring territories, led to a wave of bankruptcies. Many Koryaks caught up in what was to become only the first wave of bankruptcies—I guess that would be forty years ago now, sold or rented their herds to other up-and-coming wannabe pastoralists. Those who didn’t, sold to banks, which turned around and immediately re-sold. The second wave of bankruptcies in the 2070s hit even harder, and the now swollen ranks of neo-pastoralists faced a debt crisis that ended in widespread poverty, crippling a generation of Koryaks, with no end in sight. Alcoholism, suicide—I heard sometimes familicide—and crime skyrocketed. Though they had a recently-strengthened tradition of fierce independence, a significant minority of Koryak men were swept into the ranks of the Sakha rebels. It was work, you know?” This was the first time I had trouble discussing these matters. It was hitting too close to home. But, for Mrs. Stang’s sake, I was trying to sound as objective as an encyclopedia. It felt like discussing myself in the third person in front of my mother. And, I guess that’s exactly what it was, in a sense. I went on, “Others, sensing more opportunity with the wealthy regime in the west joined Moscow-loyalist fighters, leading to brother-against-brother warfare among the Koryaks, where both brothers are proxies for outside forces.”

“The Koryak language had been nearing extinction a century ago. Most individuals in the 20th and early 21st centuries spoke Russian, even at home, as well as a language closely related to Koryak: Chukchi, which had been the historic linga franca of the entire region. But, the resurgence in neo-traditional culture led to a generation of Koryak monoglots.” I noticed myself pronouncing the word in the traditional expat derisive tone. “That kind of linguistic and cultural insularism, of course, further exacerbated the economic and social problems that plague the Koryak people to this day.”

Having said all that, I almost—almost—wished I could have spoken to the Koryak, my captor in his own tongue. Oh captor, my captor.

Author's Note: LUCE’S EXPERIENCE IN SAKHA End of note.



Straight out of college, I went into the Peace Corps. Because of my interest in the Russian language, I was stationed in Chersky, in the Nizhnekolymsky district of extreme north-eastern Sakha, far from the locus of the conflict, which was largely limited to the south of the republic at the time. I had originally hoped to be stationed in Ukraine, and was disappointed with this appointment. Because the Corps is (mostly) perceived as an arm of the US government, I found I wasn’t able to develop genuine relationships with most of the Russians I came into contact with in the economic development work I’d originally been tasked with. However, a small part of my work was delivering meals to elderly people living in rural areas of Nizhnekolymsky. Some of these were the last speakers of the Yukaghir language, which I ended up learning. Quickly becoming disillusioned with the Peace Corps, I left and moved back to the states, eventually getting a job with the United Nations as a Russian translator. By the time I was 25, I had secured another overseas job, again in Sakha. This time, I was stationed in the capital at Yakutsk was with a UN-affiliated NGO, where I worked as a translator and conflict resolution consultant. My appointment in Yakutsk coincided with the escalation of the conflict to full-blown war. Because of the shortage of human resources and mt language proficiency, I quickly transitioned into a role as a junior negotiator. I quickly learned the Yakut language, though it isn’t related to Yukaghir or Russian.

 

While initiating a negotiation at a private residence south of Yakutsk, in the rural Aldansky Raion, I got captured by Sakha rebels. It seemed quiet, but one knock on the door, and all hell broke loose. The only things I’m good at are languages, and conflict resolution. But of course, this means…no conflict, no resolution. I left the US speaking English and Spanish, picked up Russian on the ground in Sakha, then Yukaghir, and Yakut. I eventually learned the Spanish-based Banguingui Creole, 

Author's Note: He’ll eventually learn two dialects of the Jovian language, Brazilian Portuguese, a little Mandarin, and (perhaps) the Rogue language. End of note.

I was able to get the Yakuts and Russians to treat me well as captors because I was able to befriend them. I thought of this as “negotiation skills” but in reality, I think I’m just a personable human being in spite of everything. I had to be. We moved every year when I was little. Then, in the group home, kids came and went. I never recognized this in myself. Always looked at myself as a socially awkward loner. 

Well, my captors didn’t see it that way. The rebels’ commanders found their chummy relationship with their prisoner to be unacceptable. Eventually, a monolingual Koryak—Igliklav Nutankavavovich, as it turned out—was chosen to take charge of the camp where I was held, I’m sure because they knew I didn’t speak Koryak.

I was held hostage for a total of about thirteen, almost fourteen years. My release was supposedly negotiated by the US government through Moscow, as an exchange for a number of Sakha rebels. I didn’t know it at the time, but I pieced it together that the actual details of my transport back home were arranged by my captors with the Chinese Triads. They were the things who got things done in Sakha at the time. It would appear that the Koryak was double-dealing though. Leading the Triads into a trap for ransom. Somehow, I guess, the Triads got wind of all this, and decided to liquidate the Yakuts, along with me and the Koryak. The Triads tried to dispose of the bodies of their liquidated operatives and captives because they were on their way to the US, and the Koryak is a known threat in the intelligence community. They couldn’t let me stick around to verify the connection between the Triads and the rebels. Looks bad for the Chinese. And for the rebels. 

 

 

Author's Note: ABOUT THE KORYAK End of note.



Igiklav Nutankavavovich—I didn’t learn his name until later—was my… I hesitate to say nemesis, but that’s about the size of it. Ever since they brought him on in my third year of captivity. He was beyond my negotiation skills because we didn’t share a common language, and because he treated prisoners as cattle. The Yakut guards were young, and could be creatively cruel in an immature way. By contrast, the Koryak wasn’t cruel. He was blunt and forceful. He wouldn’t tell us to get up and move, he would bash me in the face and point. If I was too slow, he would bash me again, often until I got knocked unconscious and could be dragged. The young Yakut guards feared and respected the Koryak, and encouraged me to do as ordered—mainly because they didn’t like dragging an unconscious prisoner around, most likely. They also whispered rumors about the Koryak when they thought he wasn’t around. 

The gossiping stopped when Nutankavavovich summarily executed two of them.

The details I explained weren’t a tenth of it, I thought.

 

“How does it end?” she asked.

 

“It doesn’t end. Either one side dominates and enforces misery on the other, or it just keeps going for centuries, slowing down and flaring up. It’s two guys beating each other to a pulp in the middle of the street. Eventually, both sides get tired, and the blows get softer and softer. Right now, they’re hitting each other pretty hard. But you can’t sustain that energy forever. Unfortunately, you can sustain it for generations. But not forever. Look at Northern Ireland, Israel, South Africa. The conflicts there are almost points on a spectrum. Hundreds of years into the conflict, and Northern Ireland healed. Hell, I remember when it became a tourist Mecca. But then you had the Catholic Knights, and it’s threatening to flare up again. Sakha will go the same way, and if we’re lucky, it won’t spill over into Irkutsk. But you see, it’s already starting to. Homogenization helps. Hell, it’s already Russians vs Russians in Sakha. The Yakuts are along for the ride. The Itelmen and Koryaks are barely pawns in the game. The ebb and flow of history eventually mixes us together until you can barely tell who’s on what sides. Homogenization may be the best way we have to beat the cycle. But tell that to Northern Ireland.”

 

"I always knew you would grow up to help others. You were always so full of emotion.”

 

“I didn’t really fit in with this family, did I?”

 

“I’m sorry for that, Luce. I really am,” she said. “My sister always said midwesterners are bottlers. I guess ‘canners’ would be more appropriate. In each of our souls is a shelf of dusty Ball jars filled with mushy pickled emotions.”

 

They were my foster parents so briefly. She was just being kind. 

 

Liquid ran down Mr. Stang's leg. He sat there with his mouth gaping, a long string of drool sticking to his collar before continuing down to moisten his trousers. 

 

"Baby, you're making a mess," said Mrs. Stang, putting a hand on his knee. "Johnny, Jonny?"

 

His mouth was like the giant pingoes of the northern steppe. Just enough of the auroralike lighting illuminated the inner edge so you could tell it was deep, but the deep interior was so shadow-veiled that you couldn't see the bottom. It might've been infinite.

 

Mrs. Stang shook her husband's leg, and he stammered to wakefulness.

 

Mr. Stang muttered something in Bahasa Malaysia. It sounded kind of like Tagalog, a little bit of which I had picked up while at sea with the Banguigui and their allies. I thought I recognized a couple words. I tried to interpolate some interesting meaning. But if somebody were to actually translate it, the real meaning would probably turn out very bland. Maybe it was “Mari kita pergi ke tidur.” 

Author's Note: Or “Saya harap anda faham sesetengah teh lebih dari kedai.” End of note.

Mrs. Stang turned to me and said, out of the blue, “If long life is your goal, then the best you can hope for is to eventually be the oldest person in the world. But in achieving that goal, all you've accomplished is to watch everybody you know die, one by one. Better to hope for an eventful life. Or better yet, a meaningful life.”

 

I said my goodbyes to the Stangs, and met back up with Taragan.

“Mr. Tar—targ-targa—“

“Luce, come on. Call me Ry.”

“Wh…why are you doing this for me?”

“Are you going to drive yourself?

I laughed. “Maybe,” I said. “It looks fun.”

He gave me an oh, really? look, so I continued: “I’ve conducted jet-ski raids on floating islands. I taught the leader of the Bangungui how to pilot Chinese bullet sub. I think I can handle a car.”

 

Ry let me take the wheel of the car. Because of Ry’s ties to the UN, he’d managed to get a safety override code that allows him to drive freehand, which would normally be illegal. He said that Flynet would still prevent collisions with other vehicles, but a driver could get as close to buildings as they wanted, even drive right on the ground. 

So, I took the wheel and had a little fun. I don’t know why, but suddenly, my limbic system kicked in, and I drove straight for the ground, almost in a trance. Ry wrestled back the wheel, shaken. 

Ry drop me off and left some guy to stand outside his door. It reminded him of his captivity… and I felt… protected. 

“This is your place. It’s not much to look at now, but there’s a really nice bed and a closet full of sheets and pillows. We made sure we got you a really good one. Really comfy. You can stay here as long as you want. As soon as you’re ready to look for a permanent home, just say the word.”

 

I spread out a sheet, and slept on the wooden floor.

Chapter 00: Marzipan

 

I finally realized there's nothing here for me. That’s when I started into a downward spiral, becoming a recluse, stim addict, and couch potato.

I blinked through the job offerings, and there were quite a few of them, though most were positions based on Callisto or Io. Research jobs were rare. From what I gathered, the consortium that managed trans-belt research had been deadlocked on funding issues since the first hostilities that led to the outbreak of the Sino-Brazilian war eight years ago.    	Representatives from both countries were on the board, and most of their backers attached riders to funding streams prohibiting their donations and investment capita be used towards facilities that employed “enemy civilians.”

This was’t a big deal for the mining facilities, since they were largely staffed and managed by individual countries, but it wreaked havoc with the research side, which had always been self consciously transnational. As it was, most of the researchers on the Jovian platform were Brazilian, and of course, most of the researchers were Chinese, so the same labor relations that ruled dirtside, ruled in Joviana.

With all the jobs on offer, it was daunting just sorting through them. The consortium was hiring a ton of engineers—probably ninety percent of the positions—so I could scratch those off the list pretty quickly. But that left just under a hundred other offerings. There were positions for clerical staff, which I though I could do, but would probably have me sitting in an office on an orbital station somewhere, and I’d rather be sweeping floors than be a desk jockey.

I briefly considered enrolling in pilot school so I could apply for a one of the handful of assistant copilot positions. It would be a few years of work, but a pilot definitely wouldn’t be stuck in one place. The only thing that kept me from pursuing that line of thinking was my uncertainty about rising through the highly specialized ranks. Driving a mining rig wouldn’t necessarily qualify one for piloting a drop ship, and a passenger ferry may or may not be the right kind of pilot job to get me close to the Jovian cloud platform. Besides, from what I’d seen on the Trans-Siberian railway, those with very particular specializations had a tendency to hold on to the positions for a long, long time. I talked to a Chuvash crane operator who’d been in the same position for twenty years and still going strong until a freak wind gust knocked him onto a rail spike and sent him into chronic pancreatitis. Nobody else in northern Asia was trained to operate that particular make of crane, so the dockyard was crippled until somebody completed several years of training, or the company could buy and install an new crane.

After an hour and a half of sorting, I’d whittled the list down to a dozen positions. There were vacuum technicians, logistics coordinators, a cook, a few radio operators—that was getting closer to what I was looking for—and even a dermatologist. Apparently, hydrogen sulphide exposure was a major problem on Io. But none of the jobs was really up my alley.

I powered down the screen and got dressed. I needed to get some air. And maybe a marzipan turnover.

But on my way out the door, I passed the mirror and realized my corduroys were stained from crotch to cuff. I looked like shit. And I looked like I smelled like shit.

So, I got undressed again, ordered a razor rush delivery, and showered. The buzzer arrived at my window as I was toweling off, and I nodded at it as I took the razor. It was charged and ready to go, and after filling the sink with gloppy piles of foam and whiskers, I washed off my face and was astonished with how old I looked. I looked like my dad, and absent the beard, it was clear I even had my dad’s double chin.

I walked, naked, back to the bedroom. This time, taking care not to look in the mirror, and went through the closet.

I wasn’t going to wear that stupid track suit again, and the only jeans Ramloco had supplied were marred buy an ugly orange floral pattern on one leg, and huge block letters on the other: MAREM.

Ugh.

That left a tan suit with suede-like elbows, shoulders, and knees, or half a dozen tuxes.

I went with the tan suit.

 

Kendra showed up. My sister. Last person I expected

Author's Note: She has to be mentioned earlier. End of note.

“God Lucy, you’re such a mess..”

I just looked at her, trying to make sense of the familiarity. No. It couldn’t be… Really? Kendra?

“Sorry—I’m so sorry; I know you’ve been through a lot; I shouldn’t have. I was just answering the message from Ramloco.”

Without thinking, I stepped forward and she tried to jerk away, but I put my arms around her and pulled her tight, tears dripping from my eyes.

I hugged her and buried my face in her hair. The sounds coming from my wide open mouth were inarticulate, like a laugh strangled by a yawn.

She pulled away and I feared she would flee. But instead, she put her hands on my face, digging her fingers into my beard and leaning her forehead against my chin.

“Luce, I don’t know where to begin,” she said into my chest.

I pushed her back a little so I could look into her eyes. My sister. I wagged my head in disbelief. My real sister.

The rims her hazel eyes welled with tears, and soon we were both crying with joy and loss and I couldn’t take it. I crumpled and bawled my eyes out on all fours on the wooden floor while she rubbed my back and shhhh-shhhh’d.

 

“Seriously though, we’ve got to get you changed.”

I looked at myself. It was surprising how dirty you could get yourself when there was food and things around to dirty yourself with. I wore my old clothes for so many twos and fives until I couldn’t remember when I’d worn anything different. But I never once spilled anything on them. Every morsel of food went into my mouth. More than anything, they had felt dusty, dead.

Kendra whistled, “They’re really trying to butter you up, aren’t they?”

I wandered into the bed room. She was surveying the closet.

“Look at all this,” she said. “I heard about your reception. Looks like someone’s going to be expecting you to attend a lot of those.”

“Oh god, please no.”

“He speaks!”

“Hmmmph.”

“I was beginning to think you’d lost the power of speech.”

I just stared at her.

“I’m sorry, I’m sorry,” she said, “I know you’ve been through a lot.”

I passed my had across the clothes hanging in the closet. There were so many fancy suits.

“Got some black tie events planned?” she asked.

“I have nothing planned.”

“Good, then we can go out for lunch,” she smiled. “If we can find something normal for you to wear. I am not going to take you to

wearing a tux.”

 

We found what Kendra called “a hell of a track suit” and left the apartment despite my pathetic protests. I felt like I was wearing silk pajamas.

 

“What’s he doing here?” asked Kendra as we passed the company man.

“They left him here to watch me.”

“I’m here in case Mr. Fagan needs anything.”

“What, like his butler?”

I thought my guard was interested in Kendra before he asked for her number. I don’t think she gave it to him.

“I’m a certified personal companion and supporter.”

I spent most of my days watching television.

And what I saw was amazing.

 

At first, I watched mostly cooking shows and comedy, but soon I spent several hours every morning watching the news reports. So much had changed.





 

The room had a small kitchen, and I was busy trying to make macaroni and cheese without burning it again, when I heard a report on Jupiter come on.

It was an interview with one of the researchers assigned to liaising with the floaters.

In the background, there was a window at which another researcher sat, tapping down notes onto a screen as a…thing behind the glass writhed in pale haze.

I waved the view to zoom into the researcher’s tablet.

 

Ahrm har ahrm raha, it said.

 

“Ahrm har ahrm raha,” I said. “Ahrm har ahrm raha. Ahrm har ahrm raha.”

 

Ahrm har ahrm raha.

 

I ordered a notebook and pencils, which came that evening. In the meantime, I set up alerts for anything related to the Jovians. Especially anything related to the language.

In the first few results, I learned that the Jovians were  apparently intelligent, but had no material culture. They lived their whole lives floating in the clouds. Because of the huge pressure differential in Jupiter’s atmosphere, they were only able to interact with humans if they floated uncomfortably high while the human researchers hovered uncomfortably low. The research base handled differential pressures, but the human vehicles that plunged into the atmosphere always ran the risk of failing.

There weren’t very many good pictures of the Jovians themselves. Just tentacle-like projections coming out of foggy air behind glass. Their orangy-pink…skin, I guess — seemed hazy itself, sometimes more warm in color, sometimes verging on lime green.

The researchers interviewed gave dry lectures on biochemistry. It seemed they had a lot of biologists and chemists, but very few cultural anthropologists, linguists, or diplomats.

I had a feeling that was going to bite them in the ass eventually.

Sadly—stupidly—half of the news coverage seemed to focus on the technology of the research platform…how it maintained buoyancy, what the docking procedures were like, what kinds of food the researchers ate.

I watched a two-hour documentary called “Life in the Clouds” which barely mentioned the Jovians at all.

After watching all day, I concluded, One: Only a handful of organizations bothered to send anybody to Jupiter, or even to conduct interviews of their own. They mostly just repackaged content from the existing programs. Two: Comparative linguistics was a dying field, if it wasn’t already dead.

That should’t have surprised me. Although at the UN, I was surrounded by people who specialized in the few remaining minority languages, my college career was marked by vain appeals to cognitive theorists to help me write grants for field research to record endangered tongues. Being theorists, however, they were little prepared to help me make a case to navigate the messiness of real-world language politics.

 

By the time my notebook and pencils arrived, I had exactly three programs queued up with moments of spoken or written Jovian speech. One was the report I first saw—turned out the person transcribing the alien speech was a telecommunications technician who came in and tried to talk to the Jovians as a hobby.

The main guy in charge of the cultural studies group, who appeared in the other two clips I’d uncovered, was—you guessed it—a cognitive theorist. It seemed he spent his time holding up mirrors and concocting object-recognition tests. The Jovians in the clips played along, but all the while, they were emitting audible vocalizations. They were trying to talk to us and he was having them play jumping jacks with hula hoops.

Although the audio quality was bad, I did manage to record a  couple pages of what I thought sounded like distinct words or phrases.

Their vocal apparatus made sounds surprisingly commensurate with human vocal anatomy.

 

In those days, I descended into self-indulgence. Absorbing the details of the new world I’d come to live in through television. Absorbing whatever I could of Jovian studies—not Joviana, but real Jovian studies. Hard to come by. At the same time, I absorbed calories enough to fill out my loose skin. After years of eating starvation rations, followed by months of a traditional South Pacific diet, my digestive system had a hard time with western food. Most of what I ate went right through me. My abdomen cramped daily. Still, somehow I managed to absorb calories at an alarming weight. 

In Sakha, I got used to drinking airag—fermented mare’s milk. It was hard to find good airag during wartime, except when I was stationed among the Neo-nomads or along the Chinese border. And, of course, that was never something my captors would let me have. 

The best facsimile I could come up with was proseco mixed with yoghurt

I din’t have a word for where she took me next, but I suspect the closest semantic match was “brothel”.

In order to help me function, Ry scheduled me to be fitted with a transdermal appliqué. It allowed me to connect to a whole world of digital media. This was far better than television. It reminded me of the internet of my childhood, but so much more.

It was still maddening though. Now I was stuck with an image of the Koryak saying “How may I help you?” in Swahili, in Triad leaders voice.

In desperation, I tried to cover my head with pillows, hide under the bed, in the closet, under the sink. 

The sink actually kind of blocks out the signal a bit, and I got a little bit o sleep there. 

I found that only with my head stuck inside the apartment's safe, mounted at chest-height on the wall, could I get any real peace. When angled just right, the specter of the Koryak disappeared. But how was I going to sleep standing up, half bent at the knees?

I sought out the help of an IT group, but they berated me when I didn’t know the name of my service provider. They told me it's illegal to disable internal neural networks. 
“What are you doing?” The kid asked, “Trying to evade bill collectors?”

I was tempted to pull the appliqué right off, but tentative picking at the edges was painful and prickly, so I started looking for alternatives.
After doing some research, I figured out the idea of a Faraday cage—a mesh that acts as an electromagnetic barrier. My first attempt to create one was to cut out the screen from the apartment window.

Turned out it wasn’t metal. It was polyplex or some such, not a conductor. But I wrapped it around my skull anyway. No effect. 

Next, he tried borrowing a sieve from the apartment complex's kitchen. This was better than nothing, but only by using several sieves did manage to kind of block the signal. I duct taped them around my head, and was able to get some rest, but they fell off in my sleep. And at that point, the kitchen staff grew weary of my requests and asked for their sieves back. 

Finally, I mustered the energy to go outside, to a hardware store. I bought some metal screening, ignoring the sales peoples' stares as I wrapped it around my head. 
It worked.

I spent the next several months at home, with a metal screen wrapped around my head, going back to my old routine of watching television. 

Months later, Kendra showed up again. There’s a different guard now, and this time, she brought a friend.

How does Kendra know Brian Lumiere?

I went on a  mission to get cleaned up, but dieting was too hard, and I strained an ankle on my first jog through Refugee Park.

After a few weeks, I had actually lost a little bit of weight.

The stim patch tucked behind my ear prickled wickedly. There was always slight nausea at this point, as I felt my head lighten and buzz.

My heart heaved oceanically.

The room brightened.

The air crisped.

I snapped up my papers and slapped them on the kitchen counter. I placed them in a precision grid covering the counter and stovetop. Top to bottom, left to right, with about a millimeter of separation between sheets.

My notes had been scrawled in my usual perfunctory handwriting. But even that seemed somehow neater now. The words looked almost embossed into the paper. Had I been stressed writing them? That seemed impossible.

I started reading from the top, saying each word until my pronunciation exactly matched my now-perfect memory of the alien tongue on the news reports.

My Sakha came back to me too, along with my Russian, and the bits of Yiddish I’d picked up at NYU. Somehow that part of my mind that sponged up grammar and sound became hyper-awake, and oddly, the other languages felt like they loaned themselves to the puzzle at hand.

It felt like each language was trying on the Jovian phonology like it was in a changing room at a clothing store.

  	None of them fit the structure of the sounds I’d transcribed, but something funny happened.

Between trying the Jovian sounds in each of the language structures, a new shape emerged. As if only by putting your pants on your head, and the your arms, and then your butt, could you feel out the actual shape of the pants.

I didn’t think I had anything like the real grammar of the language yet, but certain arrangements of utterances felt right and others felt off. Maybe there was just an internal logic to the words themselves that had eluded me up to now. Or maybe I was seeing ghosts.

But I read the words on the page aloud, and without knowing what I was saying, I thought I knew what order to put them in so they held meaning.

 

I was feeling pretty good in my powder blue suit.

The secretary seated me and handed me a tablet to fill out the application.

She seemed annoyed that I didn’t have the implant so I could just autopopulate the form, but I ignored her glares and tapped out all of my info. I put Brian Lumiere and Ambassador Carter as references, although I barely spoken to either, and I didn’t have their contact information.

I was expected to a drug test.

“Good,” I said, then dropped off the tablet and opened the door. “I’ll be right back,” I said, and left.

 

A crack snaked its way across the wet sidewalk, the storefront's luminescent ad loop catching its edge and making it flash like lightning.

He chuckled, “I’ve seen you. Those buzzers have eyes. You’re looking better.” He paused, “Were you really on one of those artificial island things?”

I nodded. “Not one like that.”

“You don’t go and order a soft boiled egg from a short order cook, not unless it’s specifically on the menu. “Now, the trick to a good sunny side up egg is you have to peel back the membrane from over the yolk. There’s actually two or three membranes in there, so take one tine of a fork and slide it just along the edge of the yolk membrane. That’s the strongest of the membranes, but you can still accidentally pop it easily. The closer you get to the yellow, the better. Then slide the tine up and over the yolk, scraping it gently. You may have to turn it to the light a little to see if you got it all. Scrape it a couple times until it looks almost like a matte finish. Then you cook it until the white is just hard. There was a medical pre-screening for the Jupiter crew and other workers, so I filled it out and got a message an hour later with instructions to go to a research facility downtown. The casual way to refer to it seemed to be “the Pettygrove complex”. 

I was glad thing were moving along so quickly, but I kept looking back at the first few questions of the odd survey: 

1. Do you have ancestry from any of the following areas (mark any that apply)?

	Ramsar, Iran

	Guarapari, Brazil

	Karunagappalli, India

	Arkaroola, Australia

	Yangjiang, China

2. Have you ever had received or donated bone marrow or G.I. Tract portions?

3. Do you have a compromised immune system or known allergies to immune-acting medications? 

I’d gotten used to using the transdermals, so I kept the text in front of me the whole way the first time I rode to the research center, alternating focus between the houses below and the hovering words. It looked like Portland neighborhoods were grossly mislabled. 



It was almost five miles to the complex, but after the first trip, I decided to walk. It was a nice walk, older residential neighborhoods about half the way, some restaurants with tables spilling out onto the sidewalks—I especially liked seeing the servers updating chalkboard specials, adding their own flourishes and wordplay. I wouldn’t have noticed before. 

The walk would have been nicer if it weren’t for the constant ozone-tinted breezes from cars above, but still I liked to stretch it out to two hours or more, pausing on the Hawthorne walkway to watch the river traffic, or walking the beach. Reminded me of childhood. Everything about my life since coming home—or wherever this was—reminded me of being a kid. The contemplative melancholy of just looking at the world for what it is. Learning a job I’d assumed was simple and unchallenging for most of my life also felt infantilizing, but in a way that I appreciated. Maybe it was years of being taken care of in Sakha—I hated that I thought of it that way, but it wasn’t inaccurate. I was their charge, and they were my caretakers, such as they were. The fresh start with Noe and Maas and the villagers, that was my newest childhood. The more I thought about it, the more those careless descriptions needed to shift, and the more accurate they felt: 

Portland is a new adolescence. 

The Banguingui village was infancy. 

Sakha was the womb. 

And now I’m reliving memories from an earlier life. How many times will I go through this cycle? Am I getting anywhere? Just treading the ground I’ve tread before? Or am I spiraling upward? 

The water slithered underneath, softened as my focus released its hold. I shook it off. “Luce!” I said in my sister’s voice in my head. “Come on, gotta move.” I let go of the bridge’s rusty rail and walked on, picking up my pace just a tad. 


The facility wasn’t as sterile as you’d expect. Nor were there any of the typical bland furnishings and decorations of a hospital. Just slick corporate placards and desks of neatly arranged research reports. My doctors for the day or for the week would meet me and usually skip the niceties, jumping right into a description of the routine for that day…as simple as could be. 

‘Today, we’ll do some walking exercises, followed by controlled breathing and a blood oxygen test.’ …that sort of thing.

And in just this way, they sprung it on me so casually I think I just nodded. I don’t remember the doctor’s face, but I remember his oaken voice, “Bone marrow and G.I. tract transplants from people who are already radiation resistant may be required for new staff without preexisting resistance.”

“Okay… Um…” 

“So, we’re going to start with the hardest part,” he said. “Marrow transplants are invasive, and G.I. Tract transplants can easily have complications. But we find it’s good to get over the hump. The rest is pretty easy. Do you have any questions at this point?”

“I don’t know. I will. Maybe. Down the road.”

“Understandable. You should know, there’s a chance you won’t be able or willing to go through with it all. Most people are fine, but it’s not uncommon for candidates to change their mind, so let us know if you’re uncomfortable with any procedure. We’ll give you time to think, but you can drop out of the program if you want, and even keep half of your training pay.”

“Wow.” 

“It’s a good deal,” he said. But, of course, we weren’t thinking about the same things at all. 

Before I knew it, I was leaning back into sedation, and the rest of that day was a blur.

Recovering from multiple organ transplants, and then weeks of flu-like symptoms from the gene therapy—they were remaking me with genes from people all over the world—certain areas of Iran, Brazil, China, places where radiation was naturally high. Apparently, their genes came in handy for our Jupiter mission. I wondered if the research that allowed this medical miracle ever provided any benefit to the residents of those places. 

Meanwhile, my hours at the café expanded because our manager got fired for skimming. She was transferring the value of refunds to a gift certificate in her name, I gahered. It was hard, but it was coming to an end, I was assured. Both by the café’s inexperienced young interim manager, and by the doctors at the complex.


“This is the last leg of your gene therapy. You’ve been doing well, so I don’t anticipate any bumps along the way.” It was the same one who gave me the news about the pig heart, and she had been right about that. Unexpectedly easy. 

I’ve been doing well. Good. I’ve been resigned, I suppose. 

“Now, what we’re going to do is to insert several genes from a radiation-resistant microorganism. The genes you’ve received so far have been from human populations, so that’s a little easier. In essence, what that did was to introduce a slightly different DNA repair mechanism into most of your body cells. Your treatment today, and over the next few weeks, will simply increase the efficiency of that mechanism in some of the more vulnerable cells in your body. The rest of this wasn’t experimental? Seemed unlikely to me. “We’ve been through all of this before. I agree.”

“Okay, go.”

She rattled off a list of symptoms by category: Likely, Possible, and Rare. They included peeling inside the mouth, increased desire for water but decreased ability to absorb water, sinking or darkening of the eyelids, and bloating. She seemed to be trying hard not to emphasize particularly salacious symptoms. So hard, that her very lack of emphasis on words like “stool” and “cancer sores” felt like an emphasis of its own. 

“In order for the treatments to be effective, you’ll have to take manganese supplements for the duration of your exposure to increased radiation environments.”

“Okay,” I said.

“That means daily pills for the entire time you’re inside the Jupiter station. It’s not a big deal, most people don’t have any problem keeping track of their medications, but if you don’t take them you could suffer severe complications, including permanent imparment and death so you need to commit to these terms. Do you agree, Mr. Fagan?”

“Yes. I agree.” Without a second thought. 

“Okay, then you’re all set. We’ll have your treatments out of the way in no time.”

Waking an hour before my alarm on the day of departure, I expected a crisp early chill, but instead the dawnlight was muggy and oppressive. Had I even slept? I’d stayed up late, packing and repacking my few belongings—shirts and pants totalling two outfits that seemed in reasonably good shape, my salt shaker, which I had emptied and tucked among the clothes, a pile of notebooks whose pages, both bound and stuffed-in, formed a frill worthy of any medieval regent. There were only so many ways to arrange those things, but I’d spent hours rearranging, with the news playing in my ears before giving up, lying down for a few minutes, then getting up to repack once more. 

Now I tugged the final configuration out the door, waving off Tegan’s helping hands as he escorted me through the quiet apartment hallway until we reached the front awning, where Russ already had a car waiting, and it seemed right to say some kind of goodbye. 

“I don’t know why we never talked much,” I offered. 

“Ha! You don’t? Really?” He rolled his eyes and I stood, dumb. 

Then he offered his hand, “Hey, look…you live on your own planet, you’re wrapped up in things I’ll never get my head around, but I respect you for it. You’re driven. I don’t know by what, but you’ve got something you have to do, and I do get that.

“But the thing is, I spend every day with you, maybe I see you one day, maybe I don’t. But either way, I spend most of my nights talking about you too. Looking at what little human contact you make for yourself, I feel like I’ve gotta know you better than anyone else in the world at this point.”

I let my eyes drop. “You’re right. I know.” I tried not to sound defensive, but what did it matter now? “I know I can get wrapped up in myself. It’s not that I don’t care about people. Only belatedly did another thought light on my mind—the fact that I would, very  shortly, be free of my foil baseball cap. No constant buzz in my head. No itchy, fingerdirt-grayed fringe. And no more Koryak. The thought of that made me smile so that I saw the glint of my teeth in the window.

It was about a three hour morning commuter flight from Portland International to the launch structure in Puerto Leguízamo, and Portland’s sÏticky summer stuck with us for the whole of it. I kept an eye out for the tube that supposedly cut across the entire Colombian countryside, marking the equator. But by the time Cuayacá announced itself on the flight tracker, we’d already descended into the clouds, graying out the windows streaked with needle lines of rain. 

The landing was so gentle I didn’t even notice until the airplane coupled with the space plane. Most of the other commuters disembarked at Cuayacá Airport for transfers to Quito or Bogotá, though it looked like quite a few seats were taken up by flight crew staying in Puerto Leguízamo. But after everyone else left, those few of us heading up to orbit lugged our bags along the aisle and up the short flight of stairs that unfolded through the ceiling hatch, disoriented by a brief burst of tropical air and a glimpse of sunset over forested cityscape. Then the belly hatch of the space plane swallowed us, and we all seated ourselves in the much smaller, windowless cabin. 

I never thought I’d be on a space plane. Hell, a couple of decades ago, they were only just testing the things, launching dummy cargoes and raw materials. 

From watching morning shows, I knew the principle: A long tube with no air in it to slow you down, held up by a stream of dense fluid between its walls. The whole world watched them erect it when I was a kid. Like a bouncy castle inflated by a slurry of liquid xenon and platinum fluoride or chromium chloride or something like that. The time lapsed orbital images of the launch system slowly poking its way through the opalescent clouds reminded me of a newly eclosed butterfly, expanding its wing skeleton. It was celebrated, the first of its kind. But by now, it was an antique. The morning shows these days focus on Katwe Yánchâng, “The Salt Farm” in Uganda. 

Everyone got settled in time for the pilot to make the same string of announcements as on the regular plane, adding only that we should lean back and not try to sit up because we would all feel very heavy for just under a minute. 

A gentle swaying gave way to a ka-chunk, and a shhhh, then all was silent.

And then it was like a hand pressed me into the dense foam of the seat. I guess I was supposed to feel about three times my weight, but I just felt like I put all my old weight back on. An instant of panic, then acceptance. 

That “under a minute” felt like a hell of a lot longer, but I passed the time thiking about taking my hat off and running my fingers through my hair. 

What the pilot hadn’t mentioned was the sudden lurch forward and gunshot sound of hitting the upper atmosphere at…who knows how fast? And then a passing feeling of falling, and a kick, and then just mild acceleration.  

The launch buzz cooed out, and the captain announced: “We have left the stratosphere. You may now move about the cabin.”

The air of the compartment was cool and too dry. Better than before, but I finally felt that panic of impending, irresistable, change. I’d made my decisions, and they’d led me here. I didn’t feel the need to move about the cabin. It would be a couple of days before rendezvous with the transfer-bus that would take me to Jupiter, so I might as just take my time exploring the cabin. 

I glanced at the itinerary text scrolling up the back of the chair in front of me. Earth, Callisto, Amalthea, Jupiter…all buried among acronyms I didn’t recognize:

The guy next to me was talking under his breath, whispering to his appliqué. I’d probably be a whisperer myself if I ever used the voice functions, but most people seemed to consider it rude to mumble to yourself when you could just go fully nonverbal. I tilted the bill of my hat to look out the port. I found the sense of flatness disconcerting. No stars, no landmarks to gauge our movement through space, in spite of what must be enormous speed. Leaning back, I pulled the my hat down over my eyes. The hard right angle of the seat seemed to get more comfortable, and I dozed off.


Except for the novelty of microgravity, next couple of days passed dully as any airplane ride, the half dozen passengers politely ignoring each other. 

The cabin was a mauve and maroon lounge, devoid of loose objects to toy with, and clearly designed to encourage gravitational thinking—all rectilinear, oriented as though down was down and up was up. Sticky shoes kept us on the floor, and there was no place out of reach of something to grab onto. Media controls were a reminder here and there that you were never far from appliqué information and distractions. I suppose the designers had wanted all of the passengers to remain distracted, engaged in anything other than the act of traveling through space. 

It seemed to be working. 

I didn’t speak to a single person apart from an occasional grunt of pardon. The media centers were connected to the network, so I figured I wasn’t out of the woods yet, but I did lift my hat a couple of times to see if I was still connected. And each time, the Koryak’s leather face greeted me. 

Soon enough, I would be out of range of the Earth’s dense noosphere, I thought. Soon enough. 

Docking with the bus proved surprisingly entertaining. We had to strap ourselves in, and though my seat barely afforded me a view of the port. The foily exterior of another ship clipped my view of the impossibly blank blackness as we docked, slowly moving to block out the enire window, but just before it did, for a moment, we were in shadow and the window became a dazzling black crescent studded with stars. 

My first view of space, the way I had imagined it. That would be seared into my memory forever. 

Turns out we weren’t docking directly with the bus, but rather a transport hub. Nothing more than a ring the size of a high school locker room with four oval dock doors and standing seats a score of passengers. It was full when we arrived, and I had to hang onto a rail, floating in air until a group of what I took to be asteroid miners by their rough hands and neatly pressed shirts, boarded their own bus to Lagrange 4. 

I’d barely strapped in when one of the airlocks hissed open and a clipped artificial voice with a Brazilian accent announced “Jupiter 6841”. 

I was begining to sweat. The stale air seemed to hold me still, but I wiped my brow with my hands and wiped them off on my pants. A woman strapped in beside me seemed to fidget a bit before asking, “Are you alright?”

“Um… yeah, I’m fine.”

“Are you sure you’re okay?”

“Yeah…well, I just have this problem.” I’m not sure why I was opening up. There was no time. Nothing to say anyway, but I went on… “Somebody’s trying to talk to me that I don’t want to talk to, and it’s just… I can’t…”

“Can I ask what they’re talking about?”

“No. I’m sorry, no. It’s just…”

“I find that if I tell myself to listen, even if it’s hard to hear, things aren’t always as bad as they seem.”

“You’re the linguist, go out and make first contact. If that doesn’t work, bake them a cake.” 



I suited up and went out. I carefully made my way across the pockmarked icy surface of our ship, towards the dark mass of the alien ship. 



Up close, the surface of the alien hull was metallic, but textured differently from the composites I was used to, or even the sheet metal and foil of older ships. It looked…sintered, but with regular striations. I couldn’t guess the method of manufacture. 



From here, our own ship’s surface looked like some kind of exotic moonscape from the cover of an old science fiction paperback. By comparison, the alien ship looked downright conventional. 



Over the rise, a mounded for moved. I stopped and tried to position myself in a friendly posture as best I could without floating away from the hull. As soon as I could tell for certain it was approaching me, I instinctively raised a hand in greeting, but immediately felt like a fool. Some “How”-saying missionary in a western movie. 



The alien moved smoothly across the hull, a dome with a series of small grasping feet that looked like silver lobster tails, clinging to the hull. As it crawled towards my it turned, and brought into view some kind of television screen. An oval of glass about two feet wide glowing with primary colors, shining in bright, globby patterns. If the shape of the suit were any gauge, this creature looked like a sea biscuit underneath. But that what was that screen all about? 

Author's Note: Compressed carbon—diamond “glass”. Methane clathrates may be providing the “fuel” for life. End of note.

I couldn’t take my eyes off it. I presumed this was a communications device and slowly moved my hand in a wave to see if there would be a change in the pattern. There did seem to be a fluttering and some shifts in brightness, but there was no discernible relationship to what I was doing. I tried a couple of other gestures, including a bow, which caused my suit to make a noise I thought for a second was a decoupling at my waist line. Before my heart jumped through my throat, I was able to keep composure and glance at my pressure display. No damage. 



“Well, what now?”







[Logistics of discussion…how to communicate? They invent a language…an artificial pidgin. They agree on some kind of time unit for the pidgin only—maybe the orbit of the rocky moon?]

We had a logistics of discussion…how to communicate? 

It looked as though the suited figure was trying to invent a language…an artificial pidgin. 

The first issue was to agree on some kind of time unit in-pidgin use so that we could arrange more of these meetings. 

We were able to get across the timing of the orbit of the rocky moonlet, and that provided us with a clock. We met with the alien when the moonlet passed closest to overhead at the portal entrance, every six hours or so. 


“They made up this pidgin language on the fly.”

“So, they’re linguistic geniuses?”

“Well...it didn’t work…”

Through trial and error, we figured out a flashing light system to communicate with the Rogues. This worked much better than trying to make them communicate with sounds. 










Apparently, I was going to “get” to go into the alien world. And, because I’m a sucker, I agreed.

But how were we going to make this work? Maybe the pressure suits the Rogues used could be adapted?

No, it turned out the scenario they envisioned was something more akin to a sample return mission.

“Do you have experience with high-pressure diving?” shouted Robin.

“I’m an ace submarine captain,” I said.

“Really?” she sighed. Her shaking subsided and she cracked an almost-smile. “Impressed.”

“Sure—I’ll take you around in my Chinese bullet sub sometime.”

“Wait, bullet subs?”

“Yeah, a bullet sub is…”

“No, I know what a bullet sub is. But those are most definitely not high-pressure divers. ZHG 1250 or 1645?.”

“Um, 1645 I think. What do you mean low pressure?”

“I mean, that’s shallow stuff. The pressure a bullet sub has to deal with is maybe like a few hundred kilos per square centimeter, tops. Below the surface of that planet down there…it’s probably millions of kilos. We’re talking thousands of pascals.”

“Okay, fine. I guess I'm not deep enough. Why don't you tell me how it's done.”

“Me? I have no idea. I just know the mathematics. And I know that you haven't faced gigapascal pressures before. Not on Earth. Not unless you've been a deep crust miner in one of your many past lives. How deep did you go in Jupiter?”

“Three atmospheres.”

She looked as though I’d just told her her mother was diagnosed with inoperable bone cancer.

 

As soon as the tube closed I realized my mistake. i could feel myself being upended, slotted into the portal…

As I felt myself start to upend and slide downward, I panicked. I reached for the latch, felt its glossite-like surface, started to pull out of fear, but simultaneously expecting the safety catch to prevent me. The tube jiggled slightly, and with a sudden hiss, my ears popped. Shit! I shoved the handle back in place. Of course they didn’t design it with a safety latch! My heartbeat pushed back against my popped ears. I had almost imploded myself with that second of panic. 



I had to hold it tight, but I realized I wasn’t ready for this. The pressure and the unknown were one thing, but the darkness was quite another. The ancient sample tube rasped lightly against the freshly minted portal seal. The darkness change was more felt than seen. The darkness inside the tube went from feeling hollow to feeling solid. I clutched my chest, arms shaking. My heartbeat filled the small space, as I felt my stomach fall out from under me. 



The sound of this darkness was like car wheels on a wet highway-the smooth kind of highway like we had in Canada when I was a kid. 



I turned on my handset, relieved at the dim white light. I hadn’t thought to ask about how long the descent would be. Who would I ask? The Rogues? Robin? Neither would have been able to answer. How thick was the ice? How fast was I traveling?



Though the distance between me and the surface was rapidly increasing, I could hear tube after tube being loaded and launched, and I felt some relief that I was part of a long caravan. I shined my screen light around the inside of the container. Robin had inspected every seal and latch, and assured me the interior would withstand the pressures the Rogues led us to expect. But given her impassioned attempt to talk me out of it, I assumed her assurance was just her way of making my life easier. She had hesitated, and I took that to mean she was only trying to ease my fears. Or was she trying to talk herself into letting me go? How did we know the aliens knew the actual pressures we would encounter. I mean, they live down there, but I live on Earth, yet I’d be hard pressed to tell you the difference between the pressure at the bottom of the Marianas Trench and the top of Mount Everest. 



My breathing was conscious. Slow, long breaths. 



My light should get me through the thirty or forty hours I expected to be gone, but somehow I was worried I would use up the battery if I kept it on for very long so early in my descent. 



No, damnit. Stop being neurotic. I wasn’t going to let myself second guess every decision. If I had to ration my battery, it would be later. Now was the time to occupy my mind with something-anything-other than the descent. 



The latch handle that had almost killed me-no, let’s not think about that. Don’t need to be neurotic, but there was no reason to be morbid either. Argh. Stop. Focus. 



Breathe.



The light-bathed latch handle had felt like glossine, but looked metallic. It wasn’t designed for an occupant, of course. It was just the backside of the mechanism intended to be triggered from the outside. It was unnervingly loose in its housing. The unfortunate thing about this tube was how monochrome it was, even for the lack of good lighting. The washed-out pinkness of my fingers looked bright by comparison to the gray handle, the gray walls, and the gray webbing Robin had installed for me to clip into after removing the baffles and specimen holders that had originally lined this overblown file cabinet. 



There were something that resembled pop rivets running down the back side of the tube, and slots for shelving running down the sides. This was the first piece of alien technology I had ever examined up close, and I was only the second or third person to do so, after Robin and maybe Captain Moos. I was surprised at how un-alien it was. What it reminded me of was looking a long-outdated version of something with which I was already familiar. Like an old telephone. Its purpose was obvious, but the design considerations were just not the same as those of a modern handy. The tube was clearly a sample container, complete with viewing window and a spot for a label. But the viewport was on the end, and the label was a translucent circle right in the middle of it. Obviously, they didn’t mind their view being cluttered the way a human would. 



The rivets that held the viewport in place weren’t flattened and flush with the glass-or whatever material this was-like the ports on our ship. Instead, the glass had a series of scallops cut out of it, against which the rivets fit flush. 



Oh god, how long am I going to be in here?



Ok. Think about something else. 



Robin. No. Ehrmfell. No. 



Kendra.



Fifteen years old, and sitting on the bridge at Humber Marshes. She didn’t want to be there, and neither did I. I was maybe eight or nine. She looked like a contestant on one of those kids’ game shows. All glossy lipstick and curled hair. Her coat was puffy. The girls at the home didn’t look like this. They were simple, basic. Like me. We were strangers. It was the first time we’d been reunited since I was born. I guess I wouldn’t have been a stranger to her, not exactly. I was her baby brother, all grown up. It’s funny, but I don’t think I ever considered how she must’ve experienced it until now. I imagined our parents bringing me home to a kindergarden-aged Kendra. She must’ve known the infant Luce, for those few months before we were separated. I understood that she’d been left with an aunt who refused to take care of me. I had spent years imagining what my parents looked like-in my young mind, they had been an interesting pair, improbable by anyone else’s standards, I’m sure. My imagined father a white-haired man with a pointed beard, my mother thin and willowy but with a determined brow. I knew I also had a sister, but that seemed irrelevant. So when she showed up, at the behest of our aunt, I almost refused to go with her. 



I remember her words exactly: “Come on, we don’t have to hang out long if you don’t want to.” With some prodding from one of the staff members of the group house whose name and face I forget entirely, I was convinced to take a trip to the park with her. 



Lehan had packed us both lunches, her motherliness knowing no bounds. 



Humber Marshes was familiar...it was one of the few places us kids got to “vacation” once in a while. Every year, we’d go camping, tromping through the woods, creeking. Funny, I’d almost forgotten about that. The first meeting with Kendra was the only image of that park I’d ever thought about since. 



Now I wondered what Kendra had made of her little brother sitting on that bridge. I must have been dirty, sticky, smelly. That’s how I remembered the group home. Too many hands making messes. Too few cleaning them up. 



We had sat there for a while, a warmish autumn breeze still too cool for my tastes. Hah! To think, there was a time when bone cold wasn’t second nature to me!



I don’t remember what we talked about….



A jolt to the tube knocked me out of my reverie. Were we there already? 



But no, the sound of tires on wet pavement continued. I pictured the stretches of ice we’d already traveled. When had it turned to “we”? I had felt so alone. Now, I remembered I’m going somewhere. Who will I meet? What will I say? Can I say anything? I may be walled off for now, but if we’re really at the end of our journey into the body of this cold planet, could it be that I have to dust off my linguist’s hat one more time?



The sound of the descent continued without change for long enough that I convinced myself the journey wasn’t finished. How long ago had it begun? This tube was small, and I was unsure of how long I would be in it. 



It was as uncertain as when I was hooded and led into the Siberian wilderness so long ago. Uncertain but for the familiarity of uncertainty. 



Heh. 



Okay, time to be pragmatic. I’d planned and packed my rations, but only now did I have the time to double-check. Apparently. 



I started crying. How had I gotten myself into this situation? I started laughing the tears out of my eyes. Had anyone in the history of humanity ever deliberately placed themselves in such a precarious position? Alone in the dark was status quo for our species, I suspected. But no, there was always companionship...spooning apes on a darkened savannah. Our ship wasn’t a bright oasis far from home. We were but scattered dust, to be brushed from God’s shoulders. 



Oh god, I thought, bursting out one more time into laughter. The sound of my voice shook the container. My ears popped again, and gasped a tiny, surprised gasp. I pressed my hands against the walls of my...my...my tomb. No! Not so morbid, Lucient. Stop now. Breathe. 



Breathe.







Breathe. Now, let’s think.



Why?



Shrug. 



What else is there to do?



What would a normal person do when confron… I screamed. AAAAAAAAGHHHHHHHHHH. That felt fake. I let it all out, aaaaaaaaaaaaaaa. Aaaaaa. 



No. I cried and laughed and screamed and shook, and felt a chill of almost electrical intensity run up and down my body. I was hyperventilating, but I was happy to be letting myself feel. Not letting myself. Being gripped by all that was happening. What the hell is happening to me? 



Taking stock: Plunging into pressures that wouldn’t just crush the volatiles out of my body, but would compress them into solids. My guides into the shiverless coldness were more unfathomable than the thoughts of an octopus. An octopus was downright homey by comparison. More unfathomable than than the sensations of a jellyfish-an oyster-a coral. I started hyperventilating again, but caught myself. Okay, I’m farther from Earth than any human being has ever been. So far outside the realm that we were built to inhabit that… Well, actually that would describe Robin and Brian and Moos. So far from only place in the universe that isn’t entirely destructive to human life that a small crack in the ship’s wall could pop them like a bubble. And now me, here I was, having decided to take a foray outside that tiny outpost, outside the outermost outside of nowhere. And into someplace not only not meant for humans...a place where Earth life, where matter from Earth right down to the dust under your fingernails was never meant to be. A bit of germ from a distant planet wriggling my way into a far-off planet to the incredulous laughter of some extra-universal observer spying in on this little droplet of frozen water in deep space. I. Lucient Fagan. Contaminant. 



Somewhere deep in the Sahara, a wind blows, carrying billions upon billions of pieces of dust from between the sand grains. Most fall elsewhere among the dunes, but some are carried off to sea, to be dropped in rapidly shifting dunes on the waters of the Atlantic. Some tiny fraction remain aloft, carried high into the stratosphere, to be distributed around the world. A thousand, a hundred, a dozen, ten, five, one. The last mote settles on the leaf of the last marigolds planted by an old lady in Montana before she passed away last month. So far from home, that one Saharan mote. And so close compared to me.



I. Lucient Fagan. Contaminant. 



I wondered what Kendra was up to right now. And when I would see her next.

Author's Note:  The limit of the partial pressure of oxygen is about 0.5 bar, the maximum pressure therefore is about 2.5 bar. For only some hours the pressure may be 4 to 5 bar, but nitrogen narcosis might be a problem  For higher pressures the amount of oxygen and nitrogen in the mix must be reduced and replaced by helium. Author's Note: Taravana is a disease often found among Polynesian island natives who habitually dive deep without breathing apparatus many times in close succession, usually for food or pearls.Author's Note: 1 End of note.Author's Note: 2 End of note. These free-divers may make 40 to 60 dives a day, each of 30 or 40 metres (100 to 140 feet). Taravana seems to be decompression sickness. The usual symptoms are vertigo, nausea, lethargy, paralysis and death. The word taravana is Tuamotu Polynesian for "to fall crazily". Taravana is also used to describe someone who is "crazy because of the sea”. End of note.

Author's Note: Breathing at depth can cause nitrogen narcosis and oxygen toxicity. And bone necrosis? Holding the breath while ascending after breathing at depth can cause air embolisms, burst lung, and collapsed lung. End of note.

Author's Note: Special breathing gas mixes such as trimix or heliox ameliorate the risk of decompression illness but do not eliminate it. End of note.

Author's Note: Trimix is a breathing gas consisting of oxygen, helium and nitrogen and is often used in deep commercial diving, during the deep phase of dives carried out using technical diving techniques, and in advanced recreational diving. End of note.

Author's Note: Heliox further eliminates the risk of nitrogen narcosis but introduces the risk of helium tremors below about 500 feet (150 m). End of note.

Author's Note: Atmospheric diving suits maintain body and breathing pressure at 1 bar, eliminating most of the hazards of descending, ascending, and breathing at depth. However, the rigid suits are bulky, clumsy, and very expensive. End of note.

Author's Note: Liquid breathing would not result in the saturation of body tissues with high pressure nitrogen or helium that occurs with the use of non-liquids, thus would reduce or remove the need for slow decompression. End of note.

Author's Note: All uses of liquid breathing for diving must involve total liquid ventilation (see above). Total liquid ventilation, however, has difficulty moving enough liquid to carry away CO2, because no matter how great the total pressure is, the amount of partial CO2 gas pressure available to dissolve CO2 into the breathing liquid can never be much more than the pressure at which CO2 exists in the blood (about 40 mm of mercury (Torr)). End of note.

Author's Note: At these pressures, most fluorocarbon liquids require about 70 mL/kg minute-ventilation volumes of liquid (about 5 L/min for a 70 kg adult) to remove enough CO2 for normal resting metabolism.Author's Note: 23 End of note. Author's Note:  Any increase in the diver's metabolic activity also increases CO2 production and the breathing rate, which is already at the limits of realistic flow rates in liquid breathing. However, it has been suggested that a liquid breathing system could be combined with a CO2 scrubber connected to the diver's blood supply; a US patent has been filed for such a method. End of note.

I hadn’t actually seen the Rogues directly until now. They’d set me up in a pressure-maintaining sample container meant to return samples from the surface of the planet. Here, on their ship, it was dark. Until one of them came up from what looked like a hall, lit by the light of its own body. 

As suspected, the “screen” on their space suits wasn’t a screen at all. It was a face plate. The kaleidoscope of primary colors wasn’t just the face of these beings. It was their whole body. The creature that approached moved like a rotund inchworm, squishing its way towards me. As it got closer, I could see its skin in more detail. It looked like a pile of translucent tubing with nearly spherical blobs of color moving through it. I couldn’t tell if there was a head or tail, front or back, other than that defined by its direction of motion. 



The sample tube seemed old. Very old. Cracked in places, but solid.

Their sonar sense has evolved dramatically at the expense of their other senses. The darker metal moon was only stumbled upon accidentally. But when they stumbled upon it, they assumed space was full of such chunks. An exhaustive search turned up empty. They only traveled as far as they could without losing the feeling of life they got from the reflected light of their home planet and its moon. They fly blind through space. They call themselves something like “The Metalworkers”.
