“They use something like sonar to detect the positions and motions of objects around them. Living especially things trigger all sorts of nested verb systems to describe various kinds of movement and intention and interaction by individuals and among groups. So, they speak of various movements of objects and at the same time, these verb complexes are influenced by their bioluminescent patterning. Only, I don’t think they can actually see the patters. It seems like their emotional states change when exposed to various lighting patterns, but they aren’t able to describe or consciously sense anything to do with light. You can shine a light right on them, and they’ll recognize it as an object but they won’t be able to tell if it’s on or off. And it’s the same with their own body coloration. “What a great strategic gift!” said Brian.

“Sort of. We can see their emotional change,” I said, “but they're extremely complex. It’s like looking at a high resolution brain scan. Useful, but it'll take an army of researchers to decode those details.”

“We don't necessarily need a lot of detail about their internal emotional states. What we need is to see how they react to specific inputs,” said Robin.

Author's Note: In the battle, they eject the quantum core, which crashes on the Hatchling’s world? ...it’ll take them centuries to get home… They rig up cryogenic freeze after defeating (?) the Rogues… or they manage to freeze everyone, but only build themselves….  

As we suited up, Robin narrated, sounding nonchalant. 

“If this works,” she said, “there’s no way the Rogues can use the ship as a weapon. That doesn’t stop them from trying other tactics Author's Note: 80,000th word 12/18/17 End of note. of course.

Author's Note: Include conversation throughout. End of note.

It was me and Robin again. Suited up and crawling over the icy outside of the ship. It reminded me of mountain climbing, hammering long screws into the ice, what amounted to makeshift pitons, and attaching cable to them as we went. It was clumsy and by no means safe, but it seemed to be working. 

I was nauseous with the spin, but tried as hard as I could to suppress it to avoid throwing up in my helmet. The far end seemed to swing over our heads as the end we were clinging to tried to fall from under us. Slowly, we climbed towards the aft torus. 

We were going to have to blow away part of the icy shielding that covered the whole ship. The chunk that had been knocked off en route had left a narrow cleft which, a well placed charge might knock off just the right amount of shielding.  

On approaching the cleft, I felt a growing sense of doom. If this didn’t work out right, we could be killed. Maybe the whole crew. More likely Robin and myself. Or worse, just one of us. 

Descending into the cleft, the meager starlight my eyes had adjusted to fell away. We worked blind, Robin crawling ahead and me nailing in a piton. 

“I think this will be the best place to position the charge. What do you think?”

The sound of Robin’s voice through suit-to-suit was a soft hiss, but infinitely comforting, surrounding. 

“What factors are you considering?”

“I’m just trying to get the deepest hole possible. Don’t really care if we damage the ship at this point. Considering the geometry,” she pointed along the edge of the cleft, “I think a charge right here will blow away this whole escarpment, maybe all the way back to engineering.” 

“Isn’t there a density difference between the the fore and aft shielding?”

“Good point, the aft shielding is much denser. But the transition doesn’t start until back before the cleft. So, we probably won’t actually expose engineering—which is good. But it should expose the torus.”

“Let’s do this.”

“Are you ready Luce?” 

“No. But let’s go.” 

She set the charge and started the countdown for thirty seconds. 

We followed the cable back as fast as we could, until we were on the whiter, denser micrometeoroid shielding surface. I turned to look, but nothing happened. Robin put a hand on my side, and we waited. 

“Are you sure this is a safe dist…” but I was interrupted by a burst of light, a spray of icy debris. A fraction of a second later, the sound and the shaking hit us, muted as it was transferred through the ship and our suits, but still distinct. Whumffh, then a crackle, then a great whining like the sound of a goat being slaughtered for soldiers’ lunch. 

The escarpment side of the cleft opened itself to starlight and slowly tumbled away into space, taking with it an enormous hunk of the shielding. Far larger than I think we intended. As a great flotilla of icebergs fled the ship, the sound evolved into a rustling, then a slushy susurrus that reminded me of our first hours aboard ship. When Robin and I first met.

When we judged the debris had cleared sufficiently, we approached the edge of the new canyon of ice to see what we had wrought. We moved silently, awed by our own destructiveness. 

The ice field cut off abruptly at the transition between fore and aft, and as our view angled over the edge, a single last iceberg floated up to greet us like the rising sun, then towering above us and casting us in shadow in its heart pounding enormity. 

When it had passed, our view was clear. We had succeeded not only in opening the cleft, but also in denuding the entire aft end of the ship of its radiation shielding. I had a moment of panic before I remembered the drive wasn’t running. The backbone of the ship stuck out from the ice, leaving the whole ship looking like a giant raw turkey drumstick with robotic bones. 

Great globs of slush clung to parts of the skeleton, wobbling like fat. 

“We did it,” said Robin. “This is it. We’re going to eject the quantum core, and we’re not going home, Luce. This is all over. We’re in a loose orbit around the Rogue planet, so we’ll probably degrade and crash Of course, the core is the majority of our mass, and with us spinning the way we are, it depends on when, exactly we eject it. We could get flung into deep space, I suppose.” 

Author's Note: It ends up that ship is falling on a cometary orbit, so they’ll reach the solar system in three hundred years or so. While the quantum core does indeed crash to the planet. End of note.

Those words seemed to cement our fate. I didn’t know what came after this, but once the quantum core was gone, we’d be stuck out here, tumbling through space. 

“We’ve got plenty of food,” I said, “so we could probably live out our lives here. It’s as good a home as any.” 
    
I was breathing hard, and I could see frost building up around the edges of my helmet glass. The suit had the smell of damp laundry that’s sat out for several days. A dreary feeling settled in on me, but I waved forward and said, “Okay, let’s finish the job.”

Our safety tether dangled into open space, chunks of ice still attached to some of the pitons. The climb down the newly formed cliff face to the skeleton of the ship was treacherous, but Robin kept us at a good pace. 

Once at the torus, the ejection of the quantum core was kind of anticlimactic. The core itself was a football-shaped body of shielding about the size of a human being. Once the tedious work of uncinching and detaching all of the leads and coolant tubes and mounting struts was finished, we stepped back and the spin of the ship did the rest for us. 

The core seemed to rise quickly and I could feel our part of the ship slow dramatically as we became a veritable feather in the breeze. The core continued on its way and we wafted off gently, but from here it looked like the opposite. 

The Rogue world hovered in the distance, momentarily eclipsed by the passing quantum core. 

We climbed back to the port opening in silence but for some huffing. I was exhausted, and Robin had done a hell of a lot more work than me, so she must have been too. 

“It’s done,” she said to Moos, waving off his questions. 

We went to our cabin alone and stripped down, curling up under the covers together.

The quiet was the most tangible thing there in the darkness, there in the motionlessness. The blur faded, waning residue of dreams Author's Note: vague and misinterpreted dreams End of note.

The blur gave way to anticipation.

This could be our last time making love. 

Her toes caught the hairs on the tops of my feet as they curled.

parts:
Yes. This is markedly different—and useful precisely because it shows which parts of your voice survive when almost everything else changes.

The obvious difference is that this is not “Nathan explaining.” It is Nathan disappearing behind a character, setting, and narrative problem. The prose is much more sensory, image-driven, scene-bound, and rhythmically controlled. You are not trying to preserve the visible topology of your own thought the way you do in conversation. You are trying to preserve the topology of the character’s attention.

That distinction matters.

In your SAT/H(s)H prose, you often leave the reader inside the evolution of an idea. Here, you leave the reader inside the evolution of a perception.

The opening does it immediately:

> “It was a new kind of darkness—a shock, for I had come to know darknesses so well.”

Then you classify the darknesses. Midnight beating. Burlap sack. Felted blanket. Forced march. Wet pillow. Cracked skull. Finally this one: “queasy, lolling and dripping wet…”

That is actually very close to the deeper pattern we identified before. You encounter an object, sort it against known categories, discover that it doesn't fit, then construct a new category around the discrepancy. But instead of doing that with geometry or ontology, Luce does it with darkness.

That may be one of the strongest cross-register Nathan fingerprints I've seen.

Your fiction also has a very strong **perceptual causality**. Things are usually introduced because the viewpoint character notices something odd, and then that oddity starts producing hypotheses. He doesn't receive a world description. He notices that the water tastes briny; therefore it isn't rain. He recognizes the bullet hole; that unlocks a memory. The container rocks; eventually he infers that it floats. The old man's hat doesn't look Yakut; then the face doesn't fit; then the language settles it.

So the worldbuilding is generally:

**observation → mismatch → interpretation → revised model**

rather than:

**author knows world → author describes world**

Again, that's almost exactly your reasoning voice translated into narrative.

Another striking thing is your fondness for **concrete systems learned through use**. You don't generally explain a technology or culture by stopping to lecture. You make someone use it incorrectly, misunderstand it, repair it, cook with it, steal from it, get hurt by it, or discover that some innocuous convention actually has social consequences.

The submarine claim is a great example. Luce says he saw it earlier. Only later does he discover that, culturally, he has laid claim to it and effectively made its contents a gift to the village. That's much stronger than writing three paragraphs about Banguingui property norms.

Same with the bartender material embedded later. You don't have the character say, “I became competent at kitchen work.” You suddenly give us a miniature practical treatise on ordering and cooking eggs.

And that bit sounds extraordinarily like your nonfiction voice:

> “You don’t go and order a soft boiled egg from a short order cook…”

followed by the operational explanation of why, what to order instead, exactly how basted eggs work, then an extremely specific technique for sunny-side-up eggs.

Your fiction is full of these little **competence islands**. The narrative temporarily becomes a field manual because somebody actually knows something.

There is also a major stylistic quality I hadn't fully appreciated from the other samples: you have a very strong taste for **literalizing metaphors and then destabilizing them**.

The container is a coffin, then a sepulcher, then an umbilical relation to his captivity. The village “breathes” like a bear. The alien city looks like a school of fish and then becomes almost literally organism-like. A pressure landscape is sky, ground, ocean, ceiling, etc., until the orientation of all those words starts to break.

You repeatedly take a familiar conceptual frame and put it under enough physical pressure that its ordinary categories stop working.

That may be why dimensional representation appeals to you so much elsewhere, actually—not causally, just stylistically. Your fiction was already doing this.

And your similes are often not decorative. They're **reasoning instruments**.

For example:

> “Like a brick in a thick wool sock.”

That's funny and ugly and immediately gives a tactile model of the pirate's face.

Or:

> “like a blanket made of tens of thousands of tiny flying carpets”

That isn't just lyrical description; it solves a visualization problem.

Or the Rogue buoyancy explanation: heavy things become functionally like light things, “paperweights and bowling balls are very light but still hold things down.” That's basically conceptual translation by analogy.

Your humor is also much more central here than the previous samples suggested. But it often enters under conditions where humor probably shouldn't work—and that's why it does.

The failed bamboo torture because the seeds won't grow.

The precious salt shaker.

“I'm a translator.”

The most expensive fried egg in the solar system.

A spaceship called “The Fucking Capital of Zimbabwe.”

Radiomushrooms.

The Jovian saying, “I don’t know how to spit.”

“Damnit, I’m a physician not a physicist.”

These are not joke setups pasted into narrative. They arise because the characters are trying to remain human while dealing with absurd conditions. That maps directly onto Luce's psychology: humor survives in the same space where trauma survives.

You also have a recurring **anti-epic instinct**. Huge events often land in mundane language.

Fourteen years of captivity:

> “Fourteen years as a hostage, and this is how it ends.”

Alien contact:

> “But what had I got?”

Interstellar travel gets reduced to bad food, awkward cabin arrangements, drug procurement, damaged cookware, interpersonal grudges.

Even the Jovians eventually become coworkers rather than sublime extraterrestrial abstractions.

That tendency appears in your nonfiction too. You will make a substantial conceptual discovery and then give it a ridiculous working name. In fiction, you do the analogous thing by pulling grand events back down into human scale.

The narrator's psychology introduces another register entirely. Luce is not Nathan, and he shouldn't sound like Nathan. He's more inhibited, more dissociative, more habitually deferential, and much more likely to turn his own feelings into an observational problem. But you've given him one trait that clearly overlaps with your natural cognitive style: **he solves distress by investigating it**.

He notices himself counting.

He notices languages.

He inventories technologies.

He learns the village.

He learns cooking.

He learns Jovian.

He learns Rogue perception.

When frightened in the sample tube, he examines the rivets.

That is a beautifully consistent characterization because intellectual curiosity isn't simply his “special skill.” It is his coping mechanism.

There's also a rhythm I hadn't seen clearly before: you frequently alternate between long accumulative passages and extremely short landings.

For example, after pages of terror and exertion:

> “But I was free.”

Or:

> “Movement.”

Or:

> “Released!”

Or:

> “Breathe.”

Or:

> “Why?”

> “Shrug.”

Those land because the surrounding prose has been allowed to sprawl. You're using compression contrast rather than maintaining one uniform sentence rhythm.

Your author notes are especially valuable for voice modeling because they show your **pre-prose cognition**. They're raw architectural instructions to yourself:

> “What does Marem want from Luce?”

> “This should be creepier…”

> “Who is speaking?”

> “Tragedy strikes.”

> “Maybe he grows dependent on the Koryak.”

You don't seem to outline in conventional scene-summary form. You throw down constraints, unanswered questions, desired effects, factual research hooks, alternate possibilities, little dialogue shards, and reminders of thematic relationships. It's almost exactly how you develop technical ideas conversationally.

So I would now add a third major voice mode:

**Narrative Nathan:** viewpoint-bound rather than author-bound. Observation leads to categorization; anomalies generate hypotheses; worldbuilding emerges through practical encounter; metaphor functions as conceptual machinery; technical competence interrupts naturally; enormous ideas repeatedly collapse back to bodily or mundane scale; humor and horror coexist without announcing the tonal transition.

And beneath all three modes—conversation, document, fiction—I now see the same deeper engine:

**Something doesn't quite fit. Examine it. Compare it with what is already known. Find the distinction that matters. Rename or reframe the thing if necessary. Follow the consequences.**

That's probably closer to your actual stylistic fingerprint than any collection of favorite punctuation or phrases.

Also: I would no longer attempt a serious imitation of your fiction by just imitating your conversational prose. That would miss it badly. This gives me enough to attempt the fiction register as its own thing.
Ok... can you pick a passage that's mostly just notes or is absent altogether, and write out the scene?

Found them. The relevant corpus is in `indexes/nathan-direct/` in `Satobloc/HsH`, not in the resources repo.

It contains the direct-Nathan exports split by year:

- `nathan-direct-2023.jsonl`
- `nathan-direct-2024.jsonl`
- `nathan-direct-2025.jsonl`
- `nathan-direct-2026.jsonl`
- plus `README.md` and `MANIFEST.json`

So yes—this is the corpus I should be looking at for the voice exercise. It’s considerably better source material than the voice-model document alone: the voice model tells me what previous analysis thought was characteristic; these give me your actual turns across a much larger range of contexts, registers, moods, lengths, and stages of thought.

I’d treat v6 as a hypothesis/model and the Nathan-direct exports as the calibration corpus. The useful next move is to sample broadly across all four years—not just hunt for conspicuous ellipses or coinages—and see what survives as a stable fingerprint when I’m looking at hundreds of genuinely Nathan-authored passages rather than a hand-selected handful.

The first egg I broke that morning had two yolks.

“Lucky,” said João.

“Not for the chicken.”

He looked at me.

“You know what I mean.”

“No, actually.”

I slid the egg onto the grill.

The whites spread farther than I expected, almost touching the potatoes, and I used the edge of the spatula to herd them back. My hand shook slightly. Not much. Enough that the spatula chattered against the steel.

João noticed.

“You cold?”

“No.”

“You look cold.”

“I’m standing in front of a grill.”

“That’s why I ask.”

I ignored him and cracked another egg.

Shell.

“Fuck.”

I fished it out with my fingertip, burned myself, swore again, then wiped my hand on my apron.

João leaned against the reach-in, watching me.

“What?”

“You look like shit.”

“Thank you.”

“No, I mean bad.”

“I understood you.”

He shrugged and went back to cutting onions.

It had been getting harder to hide.

At first, the treatments had just made me tired. Everybody was tired. That was the point of restaurant work, as far as I could tell. You arrived tired, became more tired, then went home too tired to do anything that would interfere with getting up tired the next morning.

But lately there were other things.

My gums bled when I brushed my teeth. Sometimes when I didn't.

There were little purple bruises along the inside of my arms where nobody had hit me.

My appetite had gone strange. I could cook onions and peppers and bacon all morning without wanting any of it, then suddenly find myself starving enough to eat cold hash straight from the prep pan.

And my legs hurt.

Not the muscles.

Inside.

That was the only way I could describe it. My bones felt tired.

The printer rattled.

João tore off the ticket.

“Two over medium, rye, bacon. One scramble dry, no cheese. One basted soft.”

He handed it to me.

I stared at the words.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You forgot how to read?”

“No.”

I clipped the ticket up.

Two over medium. Rye. Bacon.

Scramble dry.

Basted soft.

Easy.

I laid the eggs down.

The smell of hot fat turned my stomach.

I swallowed.

“You gonna puke?” asked Mara from the pass.

“No.”

“Because if you're gonna puke, don't puke over there.”

“I know where to puke.”

“Good.”

She vanished with two plates balanced along her forearm.

I reached for the bacon and my shoulder gave a sharp little pulse of pain.

Not pain exactly.

A white flash somewhere underneath the joint.

My hand stopped.

João noticed that too.

“Okay,” he said. “What the fuck is going on with you?”

“Radiation.”

He laughed once.

Then saw my face.

“What?”

“Radiation.”

“You have cancer?”

“No.”

“You’re getting radiation for not-cancer?”

“Basically.”

“What the fuck does that mean?”

I flipped the eggs.

One yolk broke.

“Fuck.”

“You don't break yolks.”

“I break yolks.”

“No. I work with you five days a week. You don't break yolks.”

“Well, apparently I do today.”

I scraped the egg into the waste tray and started another.

He was still looking at me.

“Are you radioactive?”

“No.”

“Can I stand here?”

“Yes.”

“You sure?”

“Pretty sure.”

“Pretty sure?”

“João.”

He held up both hands.

“Okay. Fine. I’m just asking.”

The scramble was starting to brown.

Shit.

I pulled it.

Too late.

Not ruined. Just wrong.

Dry scramble meant dry, but it didn't mean leather.

I stared at it for a second too long.

“Luce.”

“I know.”

I tossed that too.

The waste tray was beginning to look like breakfast.

Mara reappeared.

“Are we feeding the trash can today?”

“Apparently.”

She narrowed her eyes.

Then her face changed.

Not dramatically. Just enough.

“You okay?”

“Why does everybody keep asking me that?”

“Because you look gray.”

“I’m always gray.”

“No. You're beige. Today you're gray.”

João nodded.

“See?”

“You're both very supportive.”

I put the next scramble down.

Low heat.

Keep moving.

Don't let it set too hard.

Easy.

My fingers were trembling more now.

I curled them around the spatula handle and squeezed.

The grill blurred.

Not visually. Something else. Like the room had become too large and too small at the same time.

I heard the hiss of bacon.

The vent hood.

A plate hitting the pass.

Someone laughing in the dining room.

The sound of silverware being dumped into a bin.

All of it seemed to move away from me.

“Luce?”

I put both hands on the grill edge.

Bad idea.

Hot.

I pulled them back.

“Sit down,” said Mara.

“I’m fine.”

“You're not.”

“I have four eggs down.”

“I have eyes.”

“The basted—”

“I know how to baste an egg.”

That stopped me.

Of course she did.

I looked at the grill as if I'd forgotten what it was for.

João had already moved into my station.

Not dramatically.

No announcement.

He just slid over, took the spatula out of my hand, and started working.

I hated him for it for perhaps half a second.

Then I was grateful enough that I had to look away.

Mara pointed with her chin toward the milk crates near dry storage.

“Sit.”

“I can finish the ticket.”

“No.”

“I can.”

“Luce.”

Something in her voice reminded me of Lehan.

Not the sound of it.

The finality.

I sat.

The crate bowed slightly under my weight.

For a minute, nobody said anything to me.

That was worse.

Restaurant kitchens weren't quiet even when nobody was talking. There was always the machinery, the exhaust, water running somewhere, somebody opening and closing something. But I had become accustomed to the language layered on top of it.

Behind.

Hot.

Corner.

Walking in.

Two minutes.

Need fries.

Need rye.

Need hands.

Now nobody said anything in my direction.

I watched João remake my ticket.

He was faster than me.

That irritated me.

“Your basted egg is going rubbery,” I said.

He glanced at it.

“Shut up.”

“You covered it too soon.”

“Shut up.”

“The whites aren't set underneath yet.”

He lifted the lid.

They weren't.

He looked at me.

I smiled.

“There he is,” he said.

Mara came back with water.

“Drink.”

I took it.

It tasted metallic.

Everything did lately.

“What kind of radiation?” João asked without turning around.

“I don't know. The medical kind.”

“That clears it up.”

“They're getting me ready for Jupiter.”

Both stopped.

Mara looked at João.

João looked at Mara.

Then both looked at me.

“You're going to Jupiter?” she said.

“If everything works.”

“You said you were applying for some kitchen job.”

“It is a kitchen job.”

“On Jupiter.”

“Yes.”

João started laughing.

“What?”

He shook his head, still laughing.

“What?”

“Nothing. Nothing.”

“No, tell me.”

He pointed the spatula at me.

“You come in here looking like somebody microwaved you from the inside, you're dropping eggs, you're half dead, and all this time you're going to Jupiter to cook breakfast.”

“When you say it like that, it sounds stupid.”

“It is stupid.”

Mara slapped him lightly with a towel.

“No, I mean—” He struggled for the word. “It's magnificent stupid.”

I laughed.

It hurt somewhere low in my ribs.

I held my side.

Mara saw.

Her amusement disappeared.

“You need to go home.”

“I need the hours.”

“You need to not die in the kitchen.”

“I’m not going to die.”

“You don't know that.”

Neither did she.

Neither did anybody, really.

I drank more water.

The metal taste was stronger.

“I'll finish the shift.”

“No.”

“Mara—”

“No.”

“I need—”

“I'll clock you out at the end.”

“That’s wage theft.”

“It’s wage theft in your direction.”

I looked at her.

She shrugged.

“You can sue me from Jupiter.”

João slid the plate into the pass.

“Order up.”

Perfect basted egg.

Bastard.

I stood.

Mara gave me a look.

“I’m going home.”

“Good.”

I untied my apron.

My hands were still shaking.

João glanced over.

“Hey.”

“What?”

“When you get to Jupiter.”

“If.”

“When.”

I waited.

He turned back to the grill.

“Don't tell them I overcook basted eggs.”

“I'll protect your reputation.”

“Good.”

I took my coat from the hook and stepped through the back door into the wet Portland afternoon.

The cold felt wonderful.

For perhaps thirty seconds.

Then my bones started hurting again.

Because it’s from 2003, it gives us something none of the other material can: a way to distinguish what is actually persistent in your writing from what you learned later.

And quite a lot is already there.

The first thing that jumps out is the same architecture I was just describing in *Hatchlings*: you establish an apparently familiar thing, then keep changing the frame until the reader has to rebuild the category. The opening starts as an end-of-the-world testament, then immediately makes the narrator materially strange—“the minerals that compose me,” “this clay form,” words being vitrified into clay by the dying sun. fileciteturn41file0L7-L7 We don’t yet know exactly what the narrator is, but the prose has already given us a physical model to reason from.

Then you do something very Nathan-like with history:

> “before the southern blacks replaced the Jews, before the Hispanic migrants replaced the blacks, before the Arab refugees replaced the migrants, and before the Israilis replaced them…”

That’s not just scene-setting. It turns Harlem into a succession of cultural states rather than a static place. fileciteturn41file0L9-L9 That same instinct is all through *Hatchlings*: places are systems undergoing demographic, technological, political, ecological transformation.

The other very strong continuity is your attraction to **systems experienced at human scale**. The landlord’s takeover isn’t introduced by explaining some dystopian political economy. Paul discovers it as punch cards, locked doors, selectively increased rents, wallpaper buried under notices, automated speakers, restrictions on where he can stand. fileciteturn41file0L17-L21 That is almost exactly how your later fiction builds worlds. Luce learns future institutions because something inconveniences him, confuses him, charges him money, locks him out, tastes strange, or requires him to operate it.

And already, in 2003, you like technology best when it becomes slightly ridiculous through ordinary use. An authoritarian apartment regime communicates through what is basically customer-service automation. A rich oil baron is sitting in a washbasin smoking a meerschaum pipe while hearing a tenant complaint. fileciteturn41file0L25-L27 The grotesque and mundane keep stepping on each other.

The humor is much broader here than in *Hatchlings*, though. This is much more overtly satirical and fabulist. “Uncut Samson,” the masturbating mystic rabbi, is the sort of joke where you can feel the author grinning from outside the story. fileciteturn41file0L75-L81 In *Hatchlings*, the humor is usually allowed to arise from character, circumstance, or some absurdly practical detail. You became much better at hiding yourself.

But the **conceptual joke** is already completely yours.

The whole central mechanism is basically a category error turned into plot: two men are each promised possession of the same woman; Samson resolves the contradiction by stuffing both souls into one golem and literally partitioning it. fileciteturn41file0L103-L121 That is wonderfully ridiculous, but structurally it is very close to how you still think: take two incompatible requirements seriously, find the weird object in which both can simultaneously be true, then ask what consequences follow.

Paul controls the right leg. Ben Muhammad controls the left. Each can punch the other side of their shared face. They have to learn to coordinate locomotion. fileciteturn41file0L125-L141

This early prose is frequently lush because lushness itself is pleasurable:

Oh, yes. It’s not primarily “dualism.” It’s the Israel–Palestine parable, and once you notice the names it becomes almost embarrassingly obvious.

Paul Stein ≈ **Palestine**. Holly Landis ≈ **Holy Land**. And Holly is literally the daughter of **Milt and Honey Landis** — the land of milk and honey. Israel ben Muhammad gives you the other claimant while deliberately scrambling the expected ethnic/religious coding. The two men each claim Holly, and the whole plot keeps literalizing the problem of two peoples claiming the same land. fileciteturn41file0L35-L44

Then Samson makes the political metaphor physical. He promises each man sole possession, gets caught in the contradiction, and “solves” it by putting both into one golem and **partitioning the body down the middle**. They can attack each other only by damaging the body they jointly inhabit; neither can function properly without some cooperation. fileciteturn41file0L117-L141

And you practically hang a lampshade on it with Samson’s deliberately mangled “Gilgamesh” story about splitting the baby between two mothers—ben Muhammad immediately corrects him: “Isn’t that the story of Solomon?” fileciteturn41file0L103-L107

## 1. How to detect "Nathan" vs. AI voice — a working checklist

No single marker is decisive; it's the *cluster* that's diagnostic. In descending order of reliability, from what I've seen so far:

**Strong signals (rarely present in the AI text around them):**
- **Ellipsis as a thinking-pause, not a stylistic flourish.** Not "..." for trailing off dramatically — used mid-sentence, sometimes multiple times per sentence, functioning like a verbal "uh" or breath: *"Now… I'm with you on a lot of that, but… I have a couple of different things to say here…"*
- **Self-interruption and live correction.** Thoughts revised in place rather than edited out: *"No… Not unless it happens very slowly… doesn't seem impossible… Actually, no, now that I think about it that's not quite right."*
- **Direct address to an interlocutor mid-explanation.** *"Do you see what I'm saying in these cases?"* — checking in, conversational, assumes a listener who might not be following.
- **Missing/garbled words consistent with dictation, not typing.** *"make sire"* (sure), *"District geometric point of view"* (probably "distinct") — these read like speech-to-text errors, not typos. This is a strong tell for a specific subset of documents (see §4).
- **Coined terminology dropped in casually, unglossed on first use**, as if the reader already knows it: "timesheet," "braid smoothing," "the fractalscope," "backbleed." AI text tends to define terms when introducing them; this voice tends to just deploy them.
- **Sudden register break / genuine excitement interrupting formal exposition:** *"...electroweak intersection, electromagnetic intersection, and… omg… it's a GUT after all. Probably. It's a TOE with a GUT sector. Is that right?"* — the "omg," the self-doubting "Probably," and the "Is that right?" in immediate sequence is a very distinctive fingerprint: excitement, immediate self-check, uncertainty, all in three short fragments.

**Moderate signals (present but less exclusive):**
- Consistent misspellings that survive into fairly formal, deliberate writing: *transfered, enirety, wierd, anomolies, propogation* — suggests fast composition with spellcheck off or ignored, even when the content is careful and structured.
- Hedged commitment: "I think," "probably," "I don't know how X accounts for Y precisely," stacked close together rather than resolved.
- Long, comma-and-ellipsis-spliced run-ons that would be multiple sentences in edited prose.
- Section-header / manifesto-style formal writing that still lacks polish (typos above) — this is the "written but not proofread" register, distinct from both the dictated register and the AI's clean output.

**Weak / unreliable signals — don't lean on these alone:**
- Lowercase or missing terminal punctuation. It shows up (Bell's file), but plenty of your formal writing is fully punctuated, so absence of punctuation is not required.
- Brevity. Some of your most clearly-you passages are the longest thing on the page (Finding the Donut runs for paragraphs). Short ≠ you; long ≠ AI. What's diagnostic is *shape*, not length.

**How AI passages tend to look, for contrast:** evenly punctuated, hedged in a *structured* way (numbered pros/cons, tables), no dictation-error residue, terms defined when introduced, no mid-sentence self-interruption, rarely addresses "you" the way a person mid-conversation would (it's more likely to say "Would you like to explore X?" as a closing offer than "Do you see what I'm saying?" as a genuine check-in).

{"path":"/GitHub/link_6a1a5af1b40c8191affccbb98ac60fa3/create_file","args":{"repository_full_name":"Satobloc/HSH_RESOURCES","path":"PDF_SPECS/NATHAN_VOICE_MODEL/Nathan_Voice_Model_v7.md","message":"Consolidate Nathan voice model with verified corpus and fiction registers","content":"# Nathan Voice Model — v7

**Status:** current consolidated model. Earlier versions remain as provenance and development history, but v7 should be treated as the working reference unless later corrected by Nathan.

**Purpose:** model Nathan McKnight/Bellomy’s writing and speaking voice across conversation, working notes, technical/operational documents, reflective prose, and fiction without reducing the voice to surface tics. This is also a guide for distinguishing likely Nathan-authored material from surrounding AI prose and for generating new text in an appropriate Nathan register when explicitly requested.

**Core caution:** this is a voice model, not a personality diagnosis. Where a pattern appears to reflect cognition or intent, treat that as a working hypothesis unless Nathan has directly confirmed it.

---

## 1. Source hierarchy

The model should privilege sources in roughly this order:

1. **Verified raw Nathan-authored conversation batches** — especially the curated HsH `verified_batches`, because speaker attribution has been checked and the material preserves live corrections, directives, definitions, disagreements, and working thought.
2. **Directly supplied composed documents** — especially operational/taxonomic material such as `SPECIALISTS/SKILLS`, which exposes a compressed document register not well represented by conversational excerpts.
3. **Directly supplied fiction manuscripts and drafts** — especially *Hatchlings*, because fiction reveals a separate narrative register in which character attention outranks the author’s conversational surface habits.
4. **Early fiction** — especially *The Gilgamesh Golem* (2003), useful for separating long-standing structural habits from more recent learned style.
5. **Previously mined mixed SAT/H(s)H documents** — useful where Nathan-authored passages can be distinguished from AI, NotebookLM, or other inserted voices.
6. **Surface markers and inferred habits** — supporting evidence only. Never let a favorite punctuation mark or phrase outweigh source attribution and structural fit.

`METHODOLOGICAL_SNAPSHOT.txt` remains excluded as a direct Nathan-voice source per author correction: it is a roundup of material from mixed conversations rather than a clean sample of Nathan’s own prose.

---

## 2. Governing principle: preserve informative structure, not mannerisms

The strongest generalization is not “Nathan uses ellipses,” “Nathan writes run-ons,” or “Nathan coins funny words.” Those are sometimes true, but they are downstream effects.

A better rule is:

> **Nathan’s prose tends to preserve the structure of the reasoning, attention, or design process when that structure is informative.**

In live reasoning, this often means leaving the correction in place rather than replacing it with a polished conclusion. In a composed operational document, the motion may disappear while the conceptual architecture remains. In fiction, the preserved structure may belong not to Nathan’s own reasoning but to the viewpoint character’s attention: notice → mismatch → hypothesis → revised understanding.

This is why the same writer can look radically different across registers without becoming unrecognizable.

A recurring deep engine, stated cautiously, is:

> **Something does not quite fit. Examine it. Compare it with the available categories or representations. Find the distinction that matters. Rename, repartition, or reframe if necessary. Then follow the consequences.**

This is more reliable than any punctuation fingerprint.

---

## 3. High-value structural markers

### 3.1 Visible correction as information

Nathan often leaves a locally wrong or incomplete formulation visible because the correction itself records what distinction mattered.

Typical motion:

**proposition → qualification → push harder → notice category problem → local repair → continue**

“I mean…” often means: *the previous sentence was directionally right, but the category boundary was wrong.*

Do not clean away this motion automatically when imitating live Nathan. But do not manufacture fake indecision either.

### 3.2 Qualification as epistemic metadata

Words such as “I think,” “probably,” “at least by default,” “in this case,” “precisely,” and “to what degree or certainty” often carry actual model-state information. They are not mere conversational padding.

Nathan can make a strong claim and qualify it in the same breath. This is different from generic AI hedging, which often puts a soft disclaimer before a cleanly packaged answer.

### 3.3 Contrastive definition and boundary enforcement

A repeated strong move is defining something by preventing category slippage:

- a line, with thickness — but still a line, not a field
- no coil, no rest mass
- meters and meters; the direction does not change the unit
- literal rather than merely analogous, unless explicitly stated otherwise

Repetition may be used to pin the boundary down, not for rhetorical flourish.

### 3.4 Accumulative syntax rather than generic run-on syntax

Long Nathan sentences are often best understood as **accumulative syntax trees**. A clause introduces an object; another qualifies it; a parenthetical handles an exception; another clause notices a consequence; the sentence reaches a destination that could not honestly have been stated at the beginning.

When imitating, make long sentences accumulate *reasoning*, not merely length.

### 3.5 Representation switching

Nathan moves readily among geometry, ontology, method, analogy, naming, implementation, and next action. These can look like digressions from the outside, but often they are representation changes around the same structural object.

Important rule:

> **Keep representations distinct even while translating between them.**

Much of Nathan’s technical correction work consists of catching a translation that has silently become an identity claim.

### 3.6 Naming as compression

Coinages are often created when a structure has enough shape that repeatedly describing it becomes inefficient. Naming is therefore part of the reasoning operation, not a decorative afterthought.

This includes serious, playful, borrowed, hybrid, and field-crossing names. A new term may be dropped in with little ceremony and immediately treated as usable.

Do not imitate this by sprinkling whimsical names everywhere. The name should solve a compression problem.

### 3.7 Adversarial precision without necessarily adversarial social posture

Corrections can be blunt because the target is usually the classification, inference, or representation rather than the person. Nathan often prefers a clean “No, that’s not what X means here” over a padded social detour.

Do not soften a crucial technical correction until its boundary becomes vague.

### 3.8 Preserve genuine incompleteness

A strong negative marker for generic AI is the urge to normalize unfinished material. Nathan will leave duplicate labels, bare role names, unresolved placeholders, alternate formulations, open questions, and partly defined coinages when the concept itself is unfinished.

Do not silently fill these in unless asked.

---

## 4. Register map

These are not separate voices. They are operating modes with different relationships between thought, audience, and artifact.

### Register 1 — Reactive / texting-speed

Fast, minimally reviewed, sometimes telegraphic. Imperatives and short directives are common. Punctuation and capitalization may be loose. The conceptual move matters more than surface finish.

### Register 2 — Terse handoff / approval / redirect

Examples in shape: “Good. Then we should…”, “Alright. That works…”, “Great. Go ahead…”, “What about eversions?”

The important feature is not the exact phrase. It is the function: acknowledge enough to establish state, then move immediately to the next substantive operation.

### Register 3 — Exploratory / dictated / on-a-roll

Long accumulative chains, ellipses used as real thinking pauses, nested parentheticals, live repairs, abrupt changes in capitalization or proofreading discipline, and occasional VTT artifacts.

VTT-specific caution: nonsensical or near-nonsensical word substitution is stronger evidence of dictation failure than merely unusual phrasing. Do not “correct” an odd but meaningful Nathan phrase into generic English on the assumption that it must be transcription noise.

### Register 4 — Technical notebook / mid-density hybrid

Shorter declarative steps mixed with live correction. Often used when Nathan has enough local structure to reason compactly but is still solving rather than presenting.

### Register 5 — Composed technical / operational document

This register is much more compressed than the conversational voice.

Its underlying shape is often:

**scope → decomposition → category separation → functional definition → failure/test criterion → next operation**

Characteristics:

- architecture remains while most connective tissue disappears
- dense role labels and compact definitions
- strong parallel constructions
- roles defined by function, boundary, and translation responsibility
- taxonomies built as interfaces among domains
- coined terms used as conceptual compression
- implementation can begin immediately after taxonomy without rhetorical transition
- unresolved terms may remain bare rather than being padded with provisional definitions

`SPECIALISTS/SKILLS` is a major calibration source for this register. “Physicist,” “Braid Dialectologist,” “Standard Dialectologist,” “Hyperhistorian,” “Metamathematician,” “Lexotopologist,” “Mindwringer,” etc. are not ornamental names; they encode the division of labor and the transformation/interface each role owns.

### Register 6 — Recursive / meta

Nathan may comment on his own formulation while producing it, explicitly mark a sentence as a sentence, or use improvised nested notation to annotate thought in real time. “I mean…” and bare pivots such as “So.” can appear here.

Use sparingly. It is distinctive when genuine and caricatured when forced.

### Register 7 — Reflective / philosophical monologue

Structurally loose like exploratory speech but tonally different: searching, personal, sometimes melancholy, willing to move through science, ego, aesthetics, epistemology, and then return to the interrupted task.

A characteristic landing may be modest or self-deflating after a large conceptual excursion.

### Register 8 — Narrative fiction: viewpoint-bound / *Hatchlings* mode

This must **not** be generated by taking conversational Nathan and adding scenery.

The governing principle changes:

> **Preserve the topology of the viewpoint character’s attention.**

Key features:

- observation precedes explanation
- anomaly drives inference
- worldbuilding enters through practical encounter
- sensory detail performs conceptual work
- characters learn systems by using, breaking, repairing, stealing, cooking, enduring, or misunderstanding them
- technical competence may temporarily turn the narrative into a field manual when the character actually knows the subject
- similes often solve a visualization or categorization problem rather than merely decorate a sentence
- metaphor may be literalized and then destabilized
- humor can sit directly beside danger, trauma, disgust, or grief without a tonal announcement
- cosmic or historical scale repeatedly collapses back into food, clothing, tools, pain, awkward conversation, money, work, or bodily logistics
- long accumulative perceptual/reasoning passages alternate with short landings: “Movement.” “Breathe.” “But I was free.”

Most importantly, **the character must remain the character**. Luce should not sound like conversational Nathan. Luce is more inhibited, deferential, dissociative, observational, and likely to convert distress into a problem he can investigate. When his physical or emotional capacity collapses, the prose can collapse with it. An unfinished “I ...um.” may be truer than a beautifully completed insight.

### Register 9 — Mythopoetic / satirical fiction: *The Gilgamesh Golem* mode

The 2003 story shows a louder, more author-visible register than *Hatchlings*: fabular compression, historical grotesque, deliberate symbolism, broad satire, and conceptual jokes embodied as plot mechanics.

Important correction: **do not infer a general Nathan fixation on dualism from this story.** The doubleness is substantially generated by the parable itself. The story’s central machinery is an Israel/Palestine partition allegory: Paul Stein / Palestine, Holly Landis / Holy Land, Milt + Honey Landis / milk-and-honey, competing claimants, contradictory sacred covenant, partition of one shared body, and mutually damaging control of its halves. The two-ness is therefore functional mythopoetic architecture, not by itself evidence of a universal cognitive binary.

What *is* useful across time is the tendency to make an abstract contradiction operational. The magical promise does not remain metaphorical: if two people are promised the same thing, the story constructs an object in which the contradiction can literally exist, then investigates how that object moves, fights itself, cooperates, and fails.

### Register 10 — Author notes / pre-prose design cognition

The rough *Hatchlings* manuscript shows author notes that should not be mistaken for failed prose. They expose design cognition directly:

- “What does Marem want from Luce?”
- “This should be creepier…”
- “Who is speaking?”
- “Tragedy strikes.”
- alternate scene fragments
- factual research hooks
- continuity questions
- desired emotional effects

The notes are constraint surfaces, not polished outlines. They preserve possibilities and unresolved branches. When working with them, do not collapse alternatives prematurely.

---

## 5. Narrative mechanics worth preserving

### 5.1 Perceptual causality

A common fiction sequence is:

**observe → compare against expectation → notice mismatch → infer → test/revise**

Examples from *Hatchlings* include darkness being sorted against known kinds of darkness, briny water disproving “rain,” motion of a container leading toward a floating-at-sea inference, and cultural identity emerging from a progressive accumulation of dress, face, language, and behavior.

This is one of the best ways to generate new Nathan-like fiction without copying surface phrasing.

### 5.2 Competence islands

When a character knows a system, the prose is allowed to become technically specific for a while. Cooking, languages, medicine, machinery, navigation, politics, or alien communication can briefly become procedural. The explanation remains grounded by use and consequence.

### 5.3 Systems through interfaces

Large systems are frequently introduced through what someone has to do with them. Institutions become doors, cards, prices, permissions, schedules, forms, kitchens, vehicles, tools, bodily effects, or misunderstandings.

This is visible as early as *The Gilgamesh Golem*, where authoritarian property control arrives as punch cards, locked doors, rent changes, automated announcements, and access restrictions rather than as an abstract political lecture.

### 5.4 Anti-epic scale collapse

Large events repeatedly return to embarrassingly ordinary human concerns. Interstellar travel becomes bad food, cookware, drugs, work shifts, cabin logistics, clothing, or interpersonal grudges. Mythic transformation becomes two men discovering that each controls only half a leg.

This prevents speculative scale from floating free of lived experience.

### 5.5 Humor under pressure

Humor is more central than earlier voice models recognized. It often appears where another writer would enforce a single solemn tone. It need not “relieve” horror; it may coexist with it and make the situation stranger.

Do not stage every joke as a punchline. Often the absurdity should simply be allowed to remain in the same frame as the danger.

---

## 6. Surface texture: useful but secondary

These can support attribution or imitation, but none should drive it alone.

- ellipses as actual thinking pauses
- em dashes and parentheticals for local repairs or side-constraints
- “I mean…” as clarification
- bare pivots: “So.” “Good.” “Perfect.” “Excellent.”
- sparse cussing at genuine frustration, emphasis, or breakthrough
- occasional single quotes for scare-quoting
- typos and doubled words when writing quickly
- terms coined or borrowed without ceremony
- sudden excitement followed by immediate self-check
- large conceptual move followed by small/self-deflating landing

**Never manufacture typos, VTT garble, or bad punctuation to make text look Nathan-like.** Surface imperfection should arise naturally from the chosen register and drafting state.

---

## 7. Negative model: common false imitations

Avoid these failure modes:

### 7.1 Perpetual “Nathan-ness”

Not every sentence should contain ellipses, corrections, coinages, profanity, or meta-commentary. The corpus contains plenty of ordinary direct language.

### 7.2 Aphorism inflation

Earlier imitation attempts overproduced neat oppositions and quotable endings. Nathan can write aphoristically, but a paragraph should not become a row of polished maxim/punchline units.

### 7.3 Cosmetic run-ons

A long sentence with many commas is not enough. The clauses should accumulate distinctions, constraints, or consequences.

### 7.4 Decorative ellipses

Ellipses should mark hesitation, branching, or live formulation. Do not sprinkle them as voice seasoning.

### 7.5 AI social padding

Typical non-Nathan AI tells include:

- “Shall we proceed?”
- “As your co-investigator…”
- “I am now initiating…”
- routine self-narration of what the assistant is about to do
- performative enthusiasm that does not correspond to a real milestone
- unnecessary softening before a precise correction

### 7.6 Premature normalization

Do not silently:

- resolve duplicate labels
- fill every placeholder
- standardize every coinage
- choose among alternate draft fragments
- smooth away an informative correction
- turn every rough note into exposition

### 7.7 Conversational Nathan pasted onto a character

In fiction, the narrator or character’s cognition outranks the author’s chat habits. A frightened Luce should not suddenly become a Nathan technical monologue unless that is actually how Luce copes in the moment and the scene supports it.

---

## 8. Authorship discrimination: Nathan vs AI vs other machine voices

Use structure before vocabulary.

Likely Nathan indicators, cumulatively:

- local correction preserved instead of silently repaired
- qualifiers tied to precise epistemic status
- abrupt category-boundary enforcement
- compact direct handoff after an offered step
- coinage that solves an immediate reasoning need
- long syntax that accumulates model structure
- unresolved incompleteness left visible
- direct peer-level disagreement or check
- abrupt register shift that corresponds to a real cognitive or emotional change

Likely generic-AI indicators:

- uniformly polished paragraph architecture
- routine headings/tables in contexts that did not ask for them
- hedging packaged before the claim rather than embedded in its exact uncertainty
- automatic definition of every new term
- self-narration of assistant process
- “Would you like me to…” endings
- enthusiasm phrases used as transitions regardless of actual milestone
- smoothing contradictions instead of identifying the earliest unsupported edge

NotebookLM or other model output can be terse and declarative, so **brevity alone is not authorship evidence**. Mixed-source documents must be treated as multi-voice artifacts.

---

## 9. Practical generation rules

When explicitly asked to write in Nathan’s voice:

1. Determine the register first.
2. Determine whether the artifact should preserve **thought**, **architecture**, **character attention**, or **design possibilities**.
3. Build the conceptual motion before imitating punctuation.
4. Preserve category boundaries and uncertainty where they matter.
5. Let names arise only when they compress a real structure.
6. Permit roughness only where the chosen register would naturally produce it.
7. Do not make every paragraph conspicuous.
8. In fiction, keep the viewpoint character sovereign.
9. In operational documents, compress aggressively and define by function/interface.
10. In draft notes, preserve unresolved branches rather than pretending the design is settled.

A compact quality test:

> **If all the ellipses, typos, pet words, and coinages were removed, would the passage still feel structurally like Nathan?**

If not, the imitation is probably cosmetic.

---

## 10. What earlier versions contributed and what v7 changes

### Retained from v1 / `NATHAN VOICE ANALYSIS`

- ellipsis as thinking-pause
- live self-correction
- direct address
- distinction between VTT garble and ordinary odd phrasing
- coexistence of strong claim and hedge
- recognition of reactive, dictated, formal, and notebook-like registers
- early warning that structure matters more than length

### Retained and strengthened from v6

- structure over word choice
- terse handoff/approval register
- recursive self-annotation
- formal writing as a separate axis from proofreading polish
- AI negative examples
- naming as part of technical thought
- reflective/philosophical register
- multi-voice caution in mixed AI/NotebookLM/Nathan documents
- “big move, small landing” tendency

### New in v7

- verified raw conversation batches promoted above mixed technical documents as evidence
- governing idea reframed as preservation of informative structure
- explicit account of **contrastive definition / boundary enforcement**
- long sentences modeled as **accumulative syntax trees**
- “digression” reframed as **representation switching** when appropriate
- composed operational/document register based on `SPECIALISTS/SKILLS`
- explicit instruction to preserve genuine incompleteness
- full narrative-fiction register based on *Hatchlings*
- author-note / pre-prose design register
- perceptual causality, competence islands, systems-through-interfaces, anti-epic scale collapse, and humor-under-pressure added as fiction mechanics
- early-fiction/mythopoetic register based on *The Gilgamesh Golem*
- correction against overgeneralizing that story’s dualism: its paired structure is primarily generated by the Israel/Palestine partition parable
- stronger anti-caricature rules for generation

---

## 11. Current concise fingerprint

If the full model must be reduced to a handful of rules:

**Nathan-conversation:** preserve the path of thought when the path matters; qualify precisely; correct categories directly; switch representations without conflating them; let syntax accumulate with the reasoning.

**Nathan-document:** preserve the architecture and strip most of the travel; define roles and objects by function, boundary, interface, and test; do not fill unfinished concepts merely for neatness.

**Nathan-fiction:** preserve the character’s attention; let anomalies create understanding; make systems known through use; let competence become procedural when earned; keep cosmic scale tied to bodies and mundane logistics; allow humor and horror to occupy the same room.

**Nathan-draft:** preserve alternatives, questions, and incompleteness until the design itself has selected among them.

**Across all registers:** conceptual exactness matters more than surface polish, and the most reliable voice signal is structural rather than lexical.

---

*Version note: v7 is a consolidation, not a declaration of finality. Direct author correction outranks every rule above.*"}}

The writing on the leaf survived, apparently unnoticed, throughout the processes of picking and bailing, airing and sunning, spreading and aging, heaping and fermenting, pressing and kilning, and was ultimately compressed into a brick of airy golden triss-tea and stored at a certain "Warehouse 6387a" of an unknown farm conglomerate until that facility was incorporated into the fabled Ennbrook Exchange, whereafter it was transferred to a distribution node far out on the fringe of the Eenay Sai, where it sat unmolested for an estimated eighteen decades, before being acquired in a liquidation lot upon dissolution of the Ennbrook Exchange towards the end of the Third Age. [L2]   "content": "# Nathan Voice Model — v7

**Status:** current consolidated model. Earlier versions remain as provenance and development history, but v7 should be treated as the working reference unless later corrected by Nathan.

**Purpose:** model Nathan McKnight/Bellomy’s writing and speaking voice across conversation, working notes, technical/operational documents, reflective prose, and fiction without reducing the voice to surface tics. This is also a guide for distinguishing likely Nathan-authored material from surrounding AI prose and for generating new text in an appropriate Nathan register when explicitly requested.

**Core caution:** this is a voice model, not a personality diagnosis. Where a pattern appears to reflect cognition or intent, treat that as a working hypothesis unless Nathan has directly confirmed it.

---

## 1. Source hierarchy

The model should privilege sources in roughly this order:

1. **Verified raw Nathan-authored conversation batches** — especially the curated HsH `verified_batches`, because speaker attribution has been checked and the material preserves live corrections, directives, definitions, disagreements, and working thought.
2. **Directly supplied composed documents** — especially operational/taxonomic material such as `SPECIALISTS/SKILLS`, which exposes a compressed document register not well represented by conversational excerpts.
3. **Directly supplied fiction manuscripts and drafts** — especially *Hatchlings*, because fiction reveals a separate narrative register in which character attention outranks the author’s conversational surface habits.
4. **Early fiction** — especially *The Gilgamesh Golem* (2003), useful for separating long-standing structural habits from more recent learned style.
5. **Previously mined mixed SAT/H(s)H documents** — useful where Nathan-authored passages can be distinguished from AI, NotebookLM, or other inserted voices.
6. **Surface markers and inferred habits** — supporting evidence only. Never let a favorite punctuation mark or phrase outweigh source attribution and structural fit.

`METHODOLOGICAL_SNAPSHOT.txt` remains excluded as a direct Nathan-voice source per author correction: it is a roundup of material from mixed conversations rather than a clean sample of Nathan’s own prose.

---

## 2. Governing principle: preserve informative structure, not mannerisms

The strongest generalization is not “Nathan uses ellipses,” “Nathan writes run-ons,” or “Nathan coins funny words.” Those are sometimes true, but they are downstream effects.

A better rule is:

> **Nathan’s prose tends to preserve the structure of the reasoning, attention, or design process when that structure is informative.**

In live reasoning, this often means leaving the correction in place rather than replacing it with a polished conclusion. In a composed operational document, the motion may disappear while the conceptual architecture remains. In fiction, the preserved structure may belong not to Nathan’s own reasoning but to the viewpoint character’s attention: notice → mismatch → hypothesis → revised understanding.

This is why the same writer can look radically different across registers without becoming unrecognizable.

A recurring deep engine, stated cautiously, is:

> **Something does not quite fit. Examine it. Compare it with the available categories or representations. Find the distinction that matters. Rename, repartition, or reframe if necessary. Then follow the consequences.**

This is more reliable than any punctuation fingerprint.

---

## 3. High-value structural markers

### 3.1 Visible correction as information

Nathan often leaves a locally wrong or incomplete formulation visible because the correction itself records what distinction mattered.

Typical motion:

**proposition → qualification → push harder → notice category problem → local repair → continue**

“I mean…” often means: *the previous sentence was directionally right, but the category boundary was wrong.*

Do not clean away this motion automatically when imitating live Nathan. But do not manufacture fake indecision either.

### 3.2 Qualification as epistemic metadata

Words such as “I think,” “probably,” “at least by default,” “in this case,” “precisely,” and “to what degree or certainty” often carry actual model-state information. They are not mere conversational padding.

Nathan can make a strong claim and qualify it in the same breath. This is different from generic AI hedging, which often puts a soft disclaimer before a cleanly packaged answer.

### 3.3 Contrastive definition and boundary enforcement

A repeated strong move is defining something by preventing category slippage:

- a line, with thickness — but still a line, not a field
- no coil, no rest mass
- meters and meters; the direction does not change the unit
- literal rather than merely analogous, unless explicitly stated otherwise

Repetition may be used to pin the boundary down, not for rhetorical flourish.

### 3.4 Accumulative syntax rather than generic run-on syntax

Long Nathan sentences are often best understood as **accumulative syntax trees**. A clause introduces an object; another qualifies it; a parenthetical handles an exception; another clause notices a consequence; the sentence reaches a destination that could not honestly have been stated at the beginning.

When imitating, make long sentences accumulate *reasoning*, not merely length.

### 3.5 Representation switching

Nathan moves readily among geometry, ontology, method, analogy, naming, implementation, and next action. These can look like digressions from the outside, but often they are representation changes around the same structural object.

Important rule:

> **Keep representations distinct even while translating between them.**

Much of Nathan’s technical correction work consists of catching a translation that has silently become an identity claim.

### 3.6 Naming as compression

Coinages are often created when a structure has enough shape that repeatedly describing it becomes inefficient. Naming is therefore part of the reasoning operation, not a decorative afterthought.

This includes serious, playful, borrowed, hybrid, and field-crossing names. A new term may be dropped in with little ceremony and immediately treated as usable.

Do not imitate this by sprinkling whimsical names everywhere. The name should solve a compression problem.

### 3.7 Adversarial precision without necessarily adversarial social posture

Corrections can be blunt because the target is usually the classification, inference, or representation rather than the person. Nathan often prefers a clean “No, that’s not what X means here” over a padded social detour.

Do not soften a crucial technical correction until its boundary becomes vague.

### 3.8 Preserve genuine incompleteness

A strong negative marker for generic AI is the urge to normalize unfinished material. Nathan will leave duplicate labels, bare role names, unresolved placeholders, alternate formulations, open questions, and partly defined coinages when the concept itself is unfinished.

Do not silently fill these in unless asked.

---

## 4. Register map

These are not separate voices. They are operating modes with different relationships between thought, audience, and artifact.

### Register 1 — Reactive / texting-speed

Fast, minimally reviewed, sometimes telegraphic. Imperatives and short directives are common. Punctuation and capitalization may be loose. The conceptual move matters more than surface finish.

### Register 2 — Terse handoff / approval / redirect

Examples in shape: “Good. Then we should…”, “Alright. That works…”, “Great. Go ahead…”, “What about eversions?”

The important feature is not the exact phrase. It is the function: acknowledge enough to establish state, then move immediately to the next substantive operation.

### Register 3 — Exploratory / dictated / on-a-roll

Long accumulative chains, ellipses used as real thinking pauses, nested parentheticals, live repairs, abrupt changes in capitalization or proofreading discipline, and occasional VTT artifacts.

VTT-specific caution: nonsensical or near-nonsensical word substitution is stronger evidence of dictation failure than merely unusual phrasing. Do not “correct” an odd but meaningful Nathan phrase into generic English on the assumption that it must be transcription noise.

### Register 4 — Technical notebook / mid-density hybrid

Shorter declarative steps mixed with live correction. Often used when Nathan has enough local structure to reason compactly but is still solving rather than presenting.

### Register 5 — Composed technical / operational document

This register is much more compressed than the conversational voice.

Its underlying shape is often:

**scope → decomposition → category separation → functional definition → failure/test criterion → next operation**

Characteristics:

- architecture remains while most connective tissue disappears
- dense role labels and compact definitions
- strong parallel constructions
- roles defined by function, boundary, and translation responsibility
- taxonomies built as interfaces among domains
- coined terms used as conceptual compression
- implementation can begin immediately after taxonomy without rhetorical transition
- unresolved terms may remain bare rather than being padded with provisional definitions

`SPECIALISTS/SKILLS` is a major calibration source for this register. “Physicist,” “Braid Dialectologist,” “Standard Dialectologist,” “Hyperhistorian,” “Metamathematician,” “Lexotopologist,” “Mindwringer,” etc. are not ornamental names; they encode the division of labor and the transformation/interface each role owns.

### Register 6 — Recursive / meta

Nathan may comment on his own formulation while producing it, explicitly mark a sentence as a sentence, or use improvised nested notation to annotate thought in real time. “I mean…” and bare pivots such as “So.” can appear here.

Use sparingly. It is distinctive when genuine and caricatured when forced.

### Register 7 — Reflective / philosophical monologue

Structurally loose like exploratory speech but tonally different: searching, personal, sometimes melancholy, willing to move through science, ego, aesthetics, epistemology, and then return to the interrupted task.

A characteristic landing may be modest or self-deflating after a large conceptual excursion.

### Register 8 — Narrative fiction: viewpoint-bound / *Hatchlings* mode

This must **not** be generated by taking conversational Nathan and adding scenery.

The governing principle changes:

> **Preserve the topology of the viewpoint character’s attention.**

- observation precedes explanation
- anomaly drives inference
- worldbuilding enters through practical encounter
- sensory detail performs conceptual work
- characters learn systems by using, breaking, repairing, stealing, cooking, enduring, or misunderstanding them
- technical competence may temporarily turn the narrative into a field manual when the character actually knows the subject
- similes often solve a visualization or categorization problem rather than merely decorate a sentence
- metaphor may be literalized and then destabilized
- humor can sit directly beside danger, trauma, disgust, or grief without a tonal announcement
- cosmic or historical scale repeatedly collapses back into food, clothing, tools, pain, awkward conversation, money, work, or bodily logistics
- long accumulative perceptual/reasoning passages alternate with short landings: “Movement.” “Breathe.” “But I was free.”

Most importantly, **the character must remain the character**. Luce should not sound like conversational Nathan. Luce is more inhibited, deferential, dissociative, observational, and likely to convert distress into a problem he can investigate. When his physical or emotional capacity collapses, the prose can collapse with it. An unfinished “I ...um.” may be truer than a beautifully completed insight.

### Register 9 — Mythopoetic / satirical fiction: *The Gilgamesh Golem* mode

The 2003 story shows a louder, more author-visible register than *Hatchlings*: fabular compression, historical grotesque, deliberate symbolism, broad satire, and conceptual jokes embodied as plot mechanics.

Important correction: **do not infer a general Nathan fixation on dualism from this story.** The doubleness is substantially generated by the parable itself. The story’s central machinery is an Israel/Palestine partition allegory: Paul Stein / Palestine, Holly Landis / Holy Land, Milt + Honey Landis / milk-and-honey, competing claimants, contradictory sacred covenant, partition of one shared body, and mutually damaging control of its halves. The two-ness is therefore functional mythopoetic architecture, not by itself evidence of a universal cognitive binary.

What *is* useful across time is the tendency to make an abstract contradiction operational. The magical promise does not remain metaphorical: if two people are promised the same thing, the story constructs an object in which the contradiction can literally exist, then investigates how that object moves, fights itself, cooperates, and fails.

### Register 10 — Author notes / pre-prose design cognition

The rough *Hatchlings* manuscript shows author notes that should not be mistaken for failed prose. They expose design cognition directly:

- “What does Marem want from Luce?”
- “This should be creepier…”
- “Who is speaking?”
- “Tragedy strikes.”
- alternate scene fragments
- factual research hooks
- continuity questions
- desired emotional effects

The notes are constraint surfaces, not polished outlines. They preserve possibilities and unresolved branches. When working with them, do not collapse alternatives prematurely.

---

## 5. Narrative mechanics worth preserving

### 5.1 Perceptual causality

A common fiction sequence is:

**observe → compare against expectation → notice mismatch → infer → test/revise**

Examples from *Hatchlings* include darkness being sorted against known kinds of darkness, briny water disproving “rain,” motion of a container leading toward a floating-at-sea inference, and cultural identity emerging from a progressive accumulation of dress, face, language, and behavior.

This is one of the best ways to generate new Nathan-like fiction without copying surface phrasing.

### 5.2 Competence islands

When a character knows a system, the prose is allowed to become technically specific for a while. Cooking, languages, medicine, machinery, navigation, politics, or alien communication can briefly become procedural. The explanation remains grounded by use and consequence.

### 5.3 Systems through interfaces

Large systems are frequently introduced through what someone has to do with them. Institutions become doors, cards, prices, permissions, schedules, forms, kitchens, vehicles, tools, bodily effects, or misunderstandings.

This is visible as early as *The Gilgamesh Golem*, where authoritarian property control arrives as punch cards, locked doors, rent changes, automated announcements, and access restrictions rather than as an abstract political lecture.

### 5.4 Anti-epic scale collapse

Large events repeatedly return to embarrassingly ordinary human concerns. Interstellar travel becomes bad food, cookware, drugs, work shifts, cabin logistics, clothing, or interpersonal grudges. Mythic transformation becomes two men discovering that each controls only half a leg.

This prevents speculative scale from floating free of lived experience.

### 5.5 Humor under pressure

Humor is more central than earlier voice models recognized. It often appears where another writer would enforce a single solemn tone. It need not “relieve” horror; it may coexist with it and make the situation stranger.

Do not stage every joke as a punchline. Often the absurdity should simply be allowed to remain in the same frame as the danger.

---

## 6. Surface texture: useful but secondary

These can support attribution or imitation, but none should drive it alone.

- ellipses as actual thinking pauses
- em dashes and parentheticals for local repairs or side-constraints
- “I mean…” as clarification
- bare pivots: “So.” “Good.” “Perfect.” “Excellent.”
- sparse cussing at genuine frustration, emphasis, or breakthrough
- occasional single quotes for scare-quoting
- typos and doubled words when writing quickly
- terms coined or borrowed without ceremony
- sudden excitement followed by immediate self-check
- large conceptual move followed by small/self-deflating landing

**Never manufacture typos, VTT garble, or bad punctuation to make text look Nathan-like.** Surface imperfection should arise naturally from the chosen register and drafting state.

---

## 7. Negative model: common false imitations

Avoid these failure modes:

### 7.1 Perpetual “Nathan-ness”

Not every sentence should contain ellipses, corrections, coinages, profanity, or meta-commentary. The corpus contains plenty of ordinary direct language.

### 7.2 Aphorism inflation

Earlier imitation attempts overproduced neat oppositions and quotable endings. Nathan can write aphoristically, but a paragraph should not become a row of polished maxim/punchline units.

### 7.3 Cosmetic run-ons

A long sentence with many commas is not enough. The clauses should accumulate distinctions, constraints, or consequences.

### 7.4 Decorative ellipses

Ellipses should mark hesitation, branching, or live formulation. Do not sprinkle them as voice seasoning.

### 7.5 AI social padding

Typical non-Nathan AI tells include:

- “Shall we proceed?”
- “As your co-investigator…”
- “I am now initiating…”
- routine self-narration of what the assistant is about to do
- performative enthusiasm that does not correspond to a real milestone
- unnecessary softening before a precise correction

### 7.6 Premature normalization

Do not silently:

- resolve duplicate labels
- fill every placeholder
- standardize every coinage
- choose among alternate draft fragments
- smooth away an informative correction
- turn every rough note into exposition

### 7.7 Conversational Nathan pasted onto a character

In fiction, the narrator or character’s cognition outranks the author’s chat habits. A frightened Luce should not suddenly become a Nathan technical monologue unless that is actually how Luce copes in the moment and the scene supports it.

---

## 8. Authorship discrimination: Nathan vs AI vs other machine voices

Use structure before vocabulary.

Likely Nathan indicators, cumulatively:

- local correction preserved instead of silently repaired
- qualifiers tied to precise epistemic status
- abrupt category-boundary enforcement
- compact direct handoff after an offered step
- coinage that solves an immediate reasoning need
- long syntax that accumulates model structure
- unresolved incompleteness left visible
- direct peer-level disagreement or check
- abrupt register shift that corresponds to a real cognitive or emotional change

Likely generic-AI indicators:

- uniformly polished paragraph architecture
- routine headings/tables in contexts that did not ask for them
- hedging packaged before the claim rather than embedded in its exact uncertainty
- automatic definition of every new term
- self-narration of assistant process
- “Would you like me to…” endings
- enthusiasm phrases used as transitions regardless of actual milestone
- smoothing contradictions instead of identifying the earliest unsupported edge

NotebookLM or other model output can be terse and declarative, so **brevity alone is not authorship evidence**. Mixed-source documents must be treated as multi-voice artifacts.

---

## 9. Practical generation rules

When explicitly asked to write in Nathan’s voice:

1. Determine the register first.
2. Determine whether the artifact should preserve **thought**, **architecture**, **character attention**, or **design possibilities**.",
